    15	## One owner per host lifecycle
    16	
    17	An application owns runtime construction and disposal. A package exposes Effect programs and Layers.
    18	
    19	Typical owners:
    20	
    21	- Bun/Node CLI main;
    22	- HTTP server bootstrap;
    23	- Cloudflare Worker module/handler adapter;
    24	- browser application root;
    25	- test runner;
    26	- Alchemy entrypoint.
    27	
    28	Construct at most one long-lived runtime per independent host lifecycle. A browser and server may need separate runtimes because their environments differ.
    29	
    30	## Adapter shape
    31	
    32	Keep adapters small:
    33	
    34	```text
    35	host input
    36	  -> Schema decode
    37	  -> named Effect operation
    38	  -> provide application runtime
    39	  -> execute
    40	  -> Schema encode / host response
    41	```
    42	
    43	Do not perform domain branching, retry loops, provider calls, or manual logging in the adapter.
    44	
    45	## Runtime composition
    46	
    47	Compose Layers by dependency:
    48	
    49	1. platform services;
    50	2. Config provider;
    51	3. transport/storage/provider Layers;
    52	4. domain live Layers;
    53	5. observability Layers;
    54	6. application services;
    55	7. runtime.
    56	
    57	Memoise shared Layers according to the installed Effect API. Avoid constructing a new SDK/exporter/client for each request unless per-request lifetime is required.
    58	
    59	## Shutdown
    60	
    61	Tie runtime disposal to:
    62	
    63	- process signals for CLI/server;
    64	- framework shutdown/hot-reload lifecycle;
    65	- Worker request completion for scoped work;
    66	- test scope/finaliser;
    67	- explicit Alchemy callback lifecycle.
    68	
    69	Do not leave timers, sockets, spans, or fibres detached after shutdown.
    70	
    71	## Cloudflare Workers
    72	
    73	Treat the exported `fetch` handler as a host adapter.
    74	
    75	- Decode bindings once into a typed service/Config Layer.
    76	- Keep secrets redacted.
    77	- Use the host's incoming Effect request fibre when it supplies one; otherwise
    78	  run through the application's sole host runner.
    79	- Connect background completion to `ExecutionContext.waitUntil` or the installed platform integration.
    80	- Preserve interruption/resource finalisers within the platform constraints.
    81	- Avoid global mutable request state.
    82	
    83	Separate platform telemetry from application Effect telemetry.
    84	
    85	For the native Alchemy API, build shared Layers in the Worker-instance Scope.
    86	Each incoming request keeps its own Scope, interruption and response cleanup.
    87	The separate TanStack Website owns typed clients and one `runtime.server.ts`
    88	runner; its private binding adapter forwards requests to the same-stage API.
    89	Do not lend Effect Context or request services through TanStack, merge them
    90	into its runtime, or borrow native tracer hooks. The native API owns its request
    91	telemetry. Any frontend host-span adapter needs its own qualified owner and
    92	tests. Follow
    93	[hosted web telemetry](../../../alchemy-iac/references/effect/hosted-web-telemetry.md)
    94	for those separate lifetimes and proof limits.
    95	
    96	## Framework loaders/actions
    97	
    98	When a framework requires a Promise:
    99	
   100	- use one runtime bridge;
   101	- call one named operation;
   102	- encode only serialisable success/error data;
   103	- preserve redirects/responses as explicit protocol values;
   104	- do not return Effect services or Causes to the client.
   105	
   106	Hydration boundaries require encoded values. Never assume class instances, provider errors, or arbitrary tagged objects survive serialisation.
   107	
   108	## Browser
   109	
   110	Use a client runtime only for client-owned effects. Do not ship server secrets, provider Layers, filesystem services, or server Config.
   111	
   112	Web owners use `runtime.server.ts` and `runtime.client.ts`, with imports inside
   113	TanStack's matching environment functions. Runtime permission comes from the
   114	repository's exact allowed paths, not a filename suffix. React owns the browser
   115	Atom runtime and registry lifetime.
   116	
   117	Model browser lifecycle:
   118	
   119	- abort/interruption on navigation or unmount;
   120	- subscriptions scoped to components/routes;
   121	- transport through a typed client service;
   122	- cached state through a declared cache/store service;
   123	- telemetry with browser-safe fields.
   124	
   125	## Tests
   126	
   127	Tests may execute Effect directly through the test integration or a scoped test runtime. Do not make each test recreate unrelated live dependencies. Compose a deterministic test Layer and release it after the suite/test scope.
   128	
   129	## Runtime anti-patterns
   130	
   131	Reject:
   132	
   133	- `Effect.runPromise` inside `service.ts`;
   134	- one runtime per function call;

   137	- live Layer construction in React render;
   138	- swallowed shutdown/finaliser errors;

     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [The default](#the-default)
     6	- [Boundary test](#boundary-test)
     7	- [Host exceptions](#host-exceptions)
     8	- [Explicit exception record](#explicit-exception-record)
     9	- [Defects versus expected failures](#defects-versus-expected-failures)
    10	- [Strict review searches](#strict-review-searches)
    11	- [Do not fetishise syntax](#do-not-fetishise-syntax)
    12	
    13	## The default
    14	
    15	Use Effect whenever owned TypeScript performs or coordinates:
    16	
    17	- failure;
    18	- asynchronous work;
    19	- external input/output;
    20	- configuration;
    21	- resource acquisition/release;
    22	- time, retry, or randomness;
    23	- mutable or concurrent state;
    24	- queues, streams, or background work;
    25	- logging, tracing, or metrics.
    26	
    27	Keep plain TypeScript for total, deterministic leaf computation over decoded values.
    28	
    29	## Boundary test
    30	
    31	Ask four questions:
    32	
    33	1. Can this operation fail for an expected reason?
    34	2. Does it depend on the world outside its arguments?
    35	3. Does it have lifetime, cancellation, concurrency, or state semantics?
    36	4. Does it cross a trust or serialisation boundary?
    37	
    38	If any answer is yes, model it as Effect.
    39	
    40	## Host exceptions
    41	
    42	Frameworks may require:
    43	
    44	- a synchronous render function;
    45	- a Promise-returning loader/action;
    46	- a Worker `fetch` handler;
    47	- a Bun/Node CLI main;
    48	- a callback registration;
    49	- an Alchemy provider callback.
    50	
    51	Keep the exception at the outermost adapter:
    52	
    53	1. decode host input;
    54	2. construct a named Effect program;
    55	3. provide the application runtime/Layer;
    56	4. execute once;
    57	5. translate typed failure to the host protocol;
    58	6. tie shutdown to host lifecycle.
    59	
    60	Do not call `Effect.runPromise` in domain or package code.
    61	
    62	## Explicit exception record
    63	
    64	If owned code must use a normally forbidden construct, place a bounded comment or architecture rule that states:
    65	
    66	- host or measured constraint;
    67	- exact file/function;
    68	- why an Effect API cannot satisfy it;
    69	- how the exception is encapsulated;
    70	- test that prevents semantic leakage;
    71	- removal/review condition.
    72	
    73	Examples:
    74	
    75	- host callback must return Promise;
    76	- generated SDK type contains `any`;
    77	- native Map is measurably required inside one service;
    78	- a host requires one exact writable property during a controlled lifetime.
    79	
    80	React rendering can use Effect Array functions synchronously; it does not need a native collection exception.
    81	
    82	“Simpler” and “the SDK uses it” are not sufficient.
    83	
    84	## Defects versus expected failures
    85	
    86	Use the typed error channel for:
    87	
    88	- validation;
    89	- missing records;
    90	- provider rejection;
    91	- permissions;
    92	- timeout;
    93	- unavailable dependency;
    94	- conflict;
    95	- protocol/codec mismatch;
    96	- user cancellation when domain-relevant.
    97	
    98	Use defects only for impossible invariants, programmer bugs, or corrupted assumptions that cannot be handled meaningfully. Do not convert expected failure to `die` to make a signature look clean.
    99	
   100	## Strict review searches
   101	
   102	Search changed owned code for:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	async
   106	new Promise
   107	Promise.
   108	throw
   109	catch (
   110	fetch(
   111	process.env
   112	Bun.env
   113	import.meta.env
   114	JSON.parse
   115	JSON.stringify
   116	Date.now
   117	new Date(
   118	Math.random
   119	setTimeout
   120	setInterval
   121	console.
   122	new Map
   123	new Set
   124	 as
   125	: any
   126	Effect.run
   127	```
   128	
   129	Classify every match. Generated, vendor, fixtures, and host adapters may be excluded only through explicit path policy.
   130	
   131	## Do not fetishise syntax
   132	
   133	Strict Effect is about semantics, not maximizing `Effect.gen`.
   134	
   135	- Keep pure Effect `Array.map`/`reduce`/`unfold` transformations synchronous; they do not need Effect.gen. Use immutable values even inside a leaf.
   136	- Do not wrap a constant in `Effect.succeed` unless it participates in an Effect interface.
   137	- Do not create a Layer for a static value with no dependency/lifecycle role.
   138	- Do not split a linear program into tiny helpers just to look functional.
   139	
   140	The goal is explicit failure, dependency, lifetime, concurrency, and observability—not ceremony.
   141	
   142	An exception must name its exact repository-relative file and operation/property.
   143	Do not allow an entire file, glob, filename suffix, tests folder or package to
   144	use mutation or execute Effect. The native API already owns its request fibre
   145	and Scope; return the native Effect handler instead of adding a runner. A
   146	framework that truly requires a Promise gets one checked application runner,
   147	whose lint allowance is a complete path. A similarly named package file remains
   148	forbidden. Test both the allowed operation and a nearby forbidden operation.

   188	is Effect's [Config](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/269a7c864351231d42e6e95b7fa8f32050df3691/packages/effect/src/Config.ts)
   189	and [Schema](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/269a7c864351231d42e6e95b7fa8f32050df3691/packages/effect/src/Schema.ts),
   190	plus Alchemy's [runtime binding adapter](https://github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy-async/blob/e73c66857553a5abe045e1a66b5512cf7d39ef2e/packages/alchemy/src/Runtime.ts).
   191	
   192	## Secrets
   193	
   194	Acquire secrets as Redacted values or the installed equivalent. Unwrap only inside the smallest provider request boundary.
   195	
   196	Rules:
   197	
   198	- never convert a secret to a normal string for convenience;
   199	- never include secret values in error fields;
   200	- never interpolate secrets into logs, spans, metrics, or receipts;
   201	- never place a secret in a service's public success type;
   202	- never persist it in test snapshots;
   203	- choose the narrowest supported native authentication method; do not require
   204	  OIDC when a config-scoped read-only service token meets the approved boundary.
   205	
   206	For Alchemy deployments backed by Doppler, follow the canonical
   207	[native sources and sign-in procedure](../../../alchemy-iac/references/effect/services-config-and-errors.md#native-doppler-and-dotenv-sources).
   208	Local and hosted runs both load Doppler, then optional ignored `.env`, with shell
   209	stack settings explicitly disabled. Keep native provider sign-in separate from
   210	the settings it unlocks. Read settings through checked Config in their owning
   211	Layer; do not add another secret reader or mutate the process environment.
   212	
   213	## Secret JSON bindings
   214	
   215	When a platform binding contains JSON:
   216	
   217	1. obtain it as redacted;
   218	2. expose/unredact only inside a boundary Effect;
   219	3. decode JSON using an owned Schema;
   220	4. construct a private credentials value;
   221	5. discard the plaintext as soon as possible;
   222	6. log only credential class and safe scope.
   223	
   224	Do not use unchecked `JSON.parse`.
   225	
   226	## Configuration ownership
   227	
   228	Keep domain Config near the live Layer that owns it. A shared application config module may compose domain Config values but should not become an untyped registry of every environment key.
   229	
   230	Export reusable declarations from the owner's `config.ts` beside its Schemas.
   231	The declaration combines the Schema and key, stays lazy until yielded, and can
   232	be reused by multiple Layers. Keep cross-domain composition with an owner that
   233	can depend on all participating domains without creating a package cycle.
   234	
   235	Related settings can share an owning record Schema and Config recipe. Group
   236	them because they belong to the same client or policy; reading several settings
   237	does not by itself require a new Context service.
   238	
   239	Expose an environment key when the host needs to choose a different value for
   240	a deployment. Keep supported protocol implementations and fixed input validity
   241	rules in code. An access policy can become checked Config when deployments need
   242	different access; that does not make malformed inputs valid.
   243	
   244	Name keys consistently and document:
   245	
   246	- owner;
   247	- environment/stage scope;
   248	- secret status;
   249	- default;
   250	- validation;
   251	- rotation/reload behaviour.
   252	
   253	Avoid defaults for Production-critical identity and credentials. Missing should fail at startup.
   254	
   255	## Reloading
   256	
   257	Most application identity/config should be immutable for a runtime. If dynamic reload is required:
   258	
   259	- model it as a service or subscription;
   260	- decode every new value;
   261	- define consistency and failure behaviour;
   262	- avoid partially updated configuration;
   263	- instrument safe version/change identity.
   264	
   265	Do not poll raw environment variables on each operation.
   266	
   267	## Tests
   268	
   269	Test:
   270	
   271	- valid Config construction;
   272	- missing required keys;
   273	- refinement failure;
   274	- default policy;
   275	- redaction in logs/errors/inspection;
   276	- test provider isolation;
   277	- stage-specific key separation;
   278	- no ambient environment dependence.
     1	# Runtimes and Host Boundaries
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [One owner per host lifecycle](#one-owner-per-host-lifecycle)
     6	- [Adapter shape](#adapter-shape)
     7	- [Runtime composition](#runtime-composition)
     8	- [Shutdown](#shutdown)
     9	- [Cloudflare Workers](#cloudflare-workers)
    10	- [Framework loaders actions](#framework-loadersactions)
    11	- [Browser](#browser)
    12	- [Tests](#tests)
    13	- [Runtime anti-patterns](#runtime-anti-patterns)
    14	
    15	## One owner per host lifecycle
    16	
    17	An application owns runtime construction and disposal. A package exposes Effect programs and Layers.
    18	
    19	Typical owners:
    20	
    21	- Bun/Node CLI main;
    22	- HTTP server bootstrap;
    23	- Cloudflare Worker module/handler adapter;
    24	- browser application root;
    25	- test runner;
    26	- Alchemy entrypoint.
    27	
    28	Construct at most one long-lived runtime per independent host lifecycle. A browser and server may need separate runtimes because their environments differ.
    29	
    30	## Adapter shape
    31	
    32	Keep adapters small:
    33	
    34	```text
    35	host input
    36	  -> Schema decode
    37	  -> named Effect operation
    38	  -> provide application runtime
    39	  -> execute
    40	  -> Schema encode / host response
    41	```
    42	
    43	Do not perform domain branching, retry loops, provider calls, or manual logging in the adapter.
    44	
    45	## Runtime composition
    46	
    47	Compose Layers by dependency:
    48	
    49	1. platform services;
    50	2. Config provider;
    51	3. transport/storage/provider Layers;
    52	4. domain live Layers;
    53	5. observability Layers;
    54	6. application services;
    55	7. runtime.
    56	
    57	Memoise shared Layers according to the installed Effect API. Avoid constructing a new SDK/exporter/client for each request unless per-request lifetime is required.
    58	
    59	## Shutdown
    60	
    61	Tie runtime disposal to:
    62	
    63	- process signals for CLI/server;
    64	- framework shutdown/hot-reload lifecycle;
    65	- Worker request completion for scoped work;
    66	- test scope/finaliser;
    67	- explicit Alchemy callback lifecycle.
    68	
    69	Do not leave timers, sockets, spans, or fibres detached after shutdown.
    70	
    71	## Cloudflare Workers
    72	
    73	Treat the exported `fetch` handler as a host adapter.
    74	
    75	- Decode bindings once into a typed service/Config Layer.
    76	- Keep secrets redacted.
    77	- Use the host's incoming Effect request fibre when it supplies one; otherwise
    78	  run through the application's sole host runner.
    79	- Connect background completion to `ExecutionContext.waitUntil` or the installed platform integration.
    80	- Preserve interruption/resource finalisers within the platform constraints.
    81	- Avoid global mutable request state.
    82	
    83	Separate platform telemetry from application Effect telemetry.
    84	
    85	For the native Alchemy API, build shared Layers in the Worker-instance Scope.
    86	Each incoming request keeps its own Scope, interruption and response cleanup.
    87	The separate TanStack Website owns typed clients and one `runtime.server.ts`
    88	runner; its private binding adapter forwards requests to the same-stage API.
    89	Do not lend Effect Context or request services through TanStack, merge them
    90	into its runtime, or borrow native tracer hooks. The native API owns its request
    91	telemetry. Any frontend host-span adapter needs its own qualified owner and
    92	tests. Follow
    93	[hosted web telemetry](../../../alchemy-iac/references/effect/hosted-web-telemetry.md)
    94	for those separate lifetimes and proof limits.
    95	
    96	## Framework loaders/actions
    97	
    98	When a framework requires a Promise:
    99	
   100	- use one runtime bridge;
   101	- call one named operation;
   102	- encode only serialisable success/error data;
   103	- preserve redirects/responses as explicit protocol values;
   104	- do not return Effect services or Causes to the client.
   105	
   106	Hydration boundaries require encoded values. Never assume class instances, provider errors, or arbitrary tagged objects survive serialisation.
   107	
   108	## Browser
   109	
   110	Use a client runtime only for client-owned effects. Do not ship server secrets, provider Layers, filesystem services, or server Config.
   111	
   112	Web owners use `runtime.server.ts` and `runtime.client.ts`, with imports inside
   113	TanStack's matching environment functions. Runtime permission comes from the
   114	repository's exact allowed paths, not a filename suffix. React owns the browser
   115	Atom runtime and registry lifetime.
   116	
   117	Model browser lifecycle:
   118	
   119	- abort/interruption on navigation or unmount;
   120	- subscriptions scoped to components/routes;
   121	- transport through a typed client service;
   122	- cached state through a declared cache/store service;
   123	- telemetry with browser-safe fields.
   124	
   125	## Tests
   126	
   127	Tests may execute Effect directly through the test integration or a scoped test runtime. Do not make each test recreate unrelated live dependencies. Compose a deterministic test Layer and release it after the suite/test scope.
   128	
   129	## Runtime anti-patterns
   130	
   131	Reject:
   132	
   133	- `Effect.runPromise` inside `service.ts`;
   134	- one runtime per function call;
   135	- global runtime in a shared package;
   136	- environment reads during module import;
   137	- live Layer construction in React render;
   138	- swallowed shutdown/finaliser errors;
   139	- detached Promise background work.
     1	# Policy and Exceptions
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [The default](#the-default)
     6	- [Boundary test](#boundary-test)
     7	- [Host exceptions](#host-exceptions)
     8	- [Explicit exception record](#explicit-exception-record)
     9	- [Defects versus expected failures](#defects-versus-expected-failures)
    10	- [Strict review searches](#strict-review-searches)
    11	- [Do not fetishise syntax](#do-not-fetishise-syntax)
    12	
    13	## The default
    14	
    15	Use Effect whenever owned TypeScript performs or coordinates:
    16	
    17	- failure;
    18	- asynchronous work;
    19	- external input/output;
    20	- configuration;
    21	- resource acquisition/release;
    22	- time, retry, or randomness;
    23	- mutable or concurrent state;
    24	- queues, streams, or background work;
    25	- logging, tracing, or metrics.
    26	
    27	Keep plain TypeScript for total, deterministic leaf computation over decoded values.
    28	
    29	## Boundary test
    30	
    31	Ask four questions:
    32	
    33	1. Can this operation fail for an expected reason?
    34	2. Does it depend on the world outside its arguments?
    35	3. Does it have lifetime, cancellation, concurrency, or state semantics?
    36	4. Does it cross a trust or serialisation boundary?
    37	
    38	If any answer is yes, model it as Effect.
    39	
    40	## Host exceptions
    41	
    42	Frameworks may require:
    43	
    44	- a synchronous render function;
    45	- a Promise-returning loader/action;
    46	- a Worker `fetch` handler;
    47	- a Bun/Node CLI main;
    48	- a callback registration;
    49	- an Alchemy provider callback.
    50	
    51	Keep the exception at the outermost adapter:
    52	
    53	1. decode host input;
    54	2. construct a named Effect program;
    55	3. provide the application runtime/Layer;
    56	4. execute once;
    57	5. translate typed failure to the host protocol;
    58	6. tie shutdown to host lifecycle.
    59	
    60	Do not call `Effect.runPromise` in domain or package code.
    61	
    62	## Explicit exception record
    63	
    64	If owned code must use a normally forbidden construct, place a bounded comment or architecture rule that states:
    65	
    66	- host or measured constraint;
    67	- exact file/function;
    68	- why an Effect API cannot satisfy it;
    69	- how the exception is encapsulated;
    70	- test that prevents semantic leakage;
    71	- removal/review condition.
    72	
    73	Examples:
    74	
    75	- host callback must return Promise;
    76	- generated SDK type contains `any`;
    77	- native Map is measurably required inside one service;
    78	- a host requires one exact writable property during a controlled lifetime.
    79	
    80	React rendering can use Effect Array functions synchronously; it does not need a native collection exception.
    81	
    82	“Simpler” and “the SDK uses it” are not sufficient.
    83	
    84	## Defects versus expected failures
    85	
    86	Use the typed error channel for:
    87	
    88	- validation;
    89	- missing records;
    90	- provider rejection;
    91	- permissions;
    92	- timeout;
    93	- unavailable dependency;
    94	- conflict;
    95	- protocol/codec mismatch;
    96	- user cancellation when domain-relevant.
    97	
    98	Use defects only for impossible invariants, programmer bugs, or corrupted assumptions that cannot be handled meaningfully. Do not convert expected failure to `die` to make a signature look clean.
    99	
   100	## Strict review searches
   101	
   102	Search changed owned code for:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	async
   106	new Promise
   107	Promise.
   108	throw
   109	catch (
   110	fetch(
   111	process.env
   112	Bun.env
   113	import.meta.env
   114	JSON.parse
   115	JSON.stringify
   116	Date.now
   117	new Date(
   118	Math.random
   119	setTimeout
   120	setInterval
   121	console.
   122	new Map
   123	new Set
   124	 as
   125	: any
   126	Effect.run
   127	```
   128	
   129	Classify every match. Generated, vendor, fixtures, and host adapters may be excluded only through explicit path policy.
   130	
   131	## Do not fetishise syntax
   132	
   133	Strict Effect is about semantics, not maximizing `Effect.gen`.
   134	
   135	- Keep pure Effect `Array.map`/`reduce`/`unfold` transformations synchronous; they do not need Effect.gen. Use immutable values even inside a leaf.
   136	- Do not wrap a constant in `Effect.succeed` unless it participates in an Effect interface.
   137	- Do not create a Layer for a static value with no dependency/lifecycle role.
   138	- Do not split a linear program into tiny helpers just to look functional.
   139	
   140	The goal is explicit failure, dependency, lifetime, concurrency, and observability—not ceremony.
   141	
   142	An exception must name its exact repository-relative file and operation/property.
   143	Do not allow an entire file, glob, filename suffix, tests folder or package to
   144	use mutation or execute Effect. The native API already owns its request fibre
   145	and Scope; return the native Effect handler instead of adding a runner. A
   146	framework that truly requires a Promise gets one checked application runner,
   147	whose lint allowance is a complete path. A similarly named package file remains
   148	forbidden. Test both the allowed operation and a nearby forbidden operation.

1	# Schemas and Brands
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Decode once](#decode-once)
     6	- [Encode owned output](#encode-owned-output)
     7	- [Domain brands](#domain-brands)
     8	- [Exact structures](#exact-structures)
     9	- [Transformations](#transformations)

    11	- [Provider responses](#provider-responses)
    12	- [Schema-tagged errors](#schema-tagged-errors)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Decode once
    16	
    17	Treat all external values as `unknown` until Schema decodes them:
    18	
    19	- environment and platform bindings;
    20	- HTTP/RPC/queue input;
    21	- provider SDK responses;
    22	- database rows;
    23	- JSON files;
    24	- Alchemy state and outputs;
    25	- workflow payloads;
    26	- browser storage;
    27	- durable receipts.
    28	
    29	Decode at the first trusted boundary. Do not pass `unknown` inward for a later caller to handle.
    30	Keep the decoded value typed inside the program. Do not decode the same stage
    31	again or round-trip an internally constructed record just to establish its
    32	type. Pure construction uses the owning types and checked constructors;
    33	additional external input still needs its own boundary check. Encode when the
    34	value crosses an outward contract.
    35	
    36	## Encode owned output
    37	
    38	Use Schema encoding for:
    39	
    40	- provider requests owned by the application;
    41	- HTTP/RPC responses;
    42	- persisted state;
    43	- externally persisted cache entries (an in-memory Effect cache is already typed);
    44	- messages/events;
    45	- workflow outputs;
    46	- receipts.
    47	
    48	Encoding proves the outbound contract and prevents accidental runtime objects, Causes, secrets, or non-serialisable values from leaking.
    49	
    50	## Domain brands
    51	
    52	Brand values that are semantically distinct despite sharing a primitive:
    53	
    54	- account/project/tenant IDs;
    55	- email address;
    56	- absolute URL and redirect URI;
    57	- dataset/dashboard ID;
    58	- stage;
    59	- source revision;
    60	- money/currency;
    61	- bounded count;
    62	- timestamp and duration.
    63	
    64	Do not accept arbitrary strings and rely on parameter names to protect identity.
    65	
    66	Brand at decode/construction. Avoid a public `as Brand` escape hatch.
    67	
    68	Select the native Schema for the source data type before adding domain checks
    69	and a brand. In qualified v4, URL, numeric, duration, JSON, Option and Redacted
    70	codecs already own parsing and encoding. Use native UUID checks for UUID
    71	contracts and retain business-specific checks for other identifiers. A brand
    72	creates a distinct type; it does not validate a format by itself. See the
    73	[native Config and Schema choices](../services/config-and-secrets.md#refine-primitive-values)
    74	and recheck them against the receiving installation.
    75	
    76	## Exact structures
    77	
    78	Use exact object Schemas where unknown keys indicate drift or unsafe input. Decide deliberately whether unknown keys are rejected, stripped, or preserved; do not accept the library default without considering the boundary.
    79	
    80	Represent closed alternatives as:
    81	
    82	- literal unions;
    83	- tagged unions;
    84	- nullable/optional input that decodes into Option when absence is semantic.
    85	
    86	Use a discriminant field for plans, receipts, messages, and errors.
    87	
    88	## Transformations
    89	
    90	Use Schema transformations when encoded and domain representations differ:
    91	
    92	- ISO timestamp ↔ domain instant;
    93	- redacted encoded secret ↔ Redacted value;
    94	- string identifier ↔ brand;
    95	- nullable input ↔ Option;
    96	- provider enum ↔ domain tagged union.
    97	
    98	Keep transformations total in each declared direction or expose decode failure explicitly.
    99	
   100	## Versioned durable data
   101	
   102	Include an explicit schema version in persisted state, events, and receipts. Define migrations as decoded transformations:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	unknown
   106	  -> version discriminator
   107	  -> old Schema decode
   108	  -> migration Effect
   109	  -> current domain
   110	  -> current Schema encode
   111	```
   112	
   113	Do not mutate historical evidence to resemble the new version.
   114	
   115	For custom Alchemy resource props/attributes, use the
   116	[stored values recipe](alchemy-stored-values.md). A codec change must preserve
   117	optional values and protected secrets, remain detectable by the selected diff
   118	path, and support recovery from both saved formats. A successful no-change apply
   119	alone does not prove that historical values were converted.
   120	
   121	## Provider responses
   122	
   123	Provider SDK typings are not runtime validation.
   124	
   125	1. call the private SDK/HttpClient;
   126	2. treat response as untrusted;
   127	3. select the minimal fields;
   128	4. decode through an owned Schema;
   129	5. map codec failure to a tagged provider-payload error;
   130	6. return domain values only.
   131	
   132	This protects against SDK looseness and provider drift.
   133	
   134	## Schema-tagged errors
   135	
   136	Use the installed Effect version's Schema-tagged error class when errors cross serialisation boundaries. Keep fields bounded and safe. For purely internal errors, a non-Schema tagged data class may be sufficient.
   137	
   138	Do not serialise arbitrary `Error`, stack traces, SDK errors, or Causes.
   139	
   140	## Tests
   141	
   142	For each material Schema, test:
   143	
   144	- representative valid decode;
   145	- every refinement failure;
   146	- unknown/missing field policy;
   147	- encode/decode round-trip where applicable;
   148	- redaction;
   149	- old-version migration;
   150	- provider drift;
   151	- maximum sizes and bounded collections.
   152	
   153	Use property-based testing for identifiers, codecs, and round-trips where valuable.
   154	
   155	## One Schema owner and checked construction
   156	
   157	Infer data types from `typeof Owner.Type` and encoded types from `typeof Owner.Encoded`.
   158	Service inputs, results, provider codecs, persisted records and test Layers reuse
   159	that owner. Do not maintain a second readonly interface with the same fields.
   160	Recursive codecs may need one local recursive annotation; infer their other
   161	fields from a shared Struct and keep the annotation beside the codec.
   162	
   163	Reuse child Schemas instead of repeating their string patterns or number bounds.
   164	An ID, source revision, URL, date, offset, span or meaningful bounded text field
   165	needs its owning refinement and brand. Branded strings remain literal source
   166	text: do not trim, case-fold or normalise legal labels as part of branding.
   167	When two fields have an ordering or length relationship, keep one shared
   168	whole-record check. `Schema.Struct({ ...Owner.fields })` copies fields only;
   169	attach the owning record check explicitly to each derived ingress codec.
   170	
   171	Separate three operations:
   172	
   173	- Decode unknown external data at its first real boundary.
   174	- Construct a new constrained value using its owner's `makeEffect` (or the
   175	  installed equivalent). In qualified v4, this checks the type side and fails
   176	  with `SchemaIssue.Issue`, not `SchemaError`; map it to the operation's safe
   177	  named error. Check child brands before constructing a containing record.
   178	- Assemble unchanged records directly from already checked fields. Retain
   179	  business checks such as expected identity, completeness and allowed ranges.
   180	
   181	A typed service input is not fresh unknown data. Do not decode it again to
   182	restore confidence, encode it and decode it to get a type, or copy a codec
   183	locally. New external input still needs checking. Native HTTP/RPC codecs can
   184	own ingress and egress without a second decoder in the semantic service.
   185	
   186	## Optional historical source data
   187	
   188	Domain readers use Option. The source codec owns the saved representation.
   189	For a record key whose source can be omitted or null, v4 supports
   190	`Schema.OptionFromOptionalKey(Schema.OptionFromNullOr(Value))`. The outer Option
   191	preserves omission; the inner Option preserves a present null. A consumer can
   192	flatten these when both mean absence, while encoding can reproduce the source.
   193	If the source does not distinguish those cases, use its simpler matching codec.
   194	
   195	Check known attributes with owning Schemas. Preserve extra JSON only as bounded,
   196	checked source evidence; do not interpret its raw values in a renderer or service.
   197	Check dictionary/rest-field codec behaviour against the installed version rather
   198	than assuming an optional-key codec also works for a Record index.
   199	
   200	Before changing an existing codec, reproduce representative old bytes, encoded
   201	field order, nulls/omissions, literal labels, saved version and cryptographic
   202	hashes. Whole-source and important subsection tests protect different claims.
   203	Effect's ordinary Hash is for collection lookup, not durable source evidence.
     1	# Errors and Causes
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Closed expected error vocabulary](#closed-expected-error-vocabulary)
     6	- [Expected failure versus defect](#expected-failure-versus-defect)
     7	- [Error fields](#error-fields)
     8	- [Boundary mapping](#boundary-mapping)
     9	- [Recovery](#recovery)
    10	- [Cause handling](#cause-handling)
    11	- [HTTP RPC translation](#httprpc-translation)
    12	- [Tests](#tests)
    13	
    14	## Closed expected error vocabulary
    15	
    16	Define domain errors in `errors.ts`. Each tag should support a caller decision.
    17	
    18	Good tags:
    19	
    20	- `AccountNotFound`;
    21	- `InvalidAccountInput`;
    22	- `ProviderUnavailable`;
    23	- `ProviderRejected`;
    24	- `ProviderPayloadInvalid`;
    25	- `PermissionDenied`;
    26	- `Conflict`;
    27	- `OperationTimedOut`;
    28	- `PersistenceFailure`.
    29	
    30	Weak tags:
    31	
    32	- `SomethingWentWrong`;
    33	- `ApiError`;
    34	- `UnknownError`;
    35	- `OperationFailed` with only a message.
    36	
    37	Do not use an error hierarchy merely to mimic exceptions. Prefer a tagged union that callers exhaustively match.
    38	
    39	## Expected failure versus defect
    40	
    41	Use typed failure for conditions that can occur in correct operation and may be handled, retried, translated, or reported.
    42	
    43	Use defects for programmer bugs or impossible invariant violations. Let supervisors/reporting capture them; do not expose them as normal domain errors.
    44	
    45	Do not catch all Causes and turn them into one expected error. Preserve interruption and defect semantics.
    46	
    47	## Error fields
    48	
    49	Include:
    50	
    51	- safe operation name;
    52	- bounded resource/provider safe ID;
    53	- retry classification;
    54	- status/code if safe and stable;
    55	- short sanitised detail;
    56	- nested domain cause only when it is a closed safe type.
    57	
    58	Exclude:
    59	
    60	- credentials;
    61	- headers/cookies;
    62	- full URLs with sensitive query strings;
    63	- raw request/response bodies;
    64	- stack traces in serialised form;
    65	- arbitrary provider error object;
    66	- unbounded messages.
    67	
    68	## Boundary mapping
    69	
    70	Map low-level errors once:
    71	
    72	```text
    73	transport failure
    74	  -> ProviderUnavailable
    75	HTTP 401/403
    76	  -> PermissionDenied
    77	HTTP 409
    78	  -> Conflict
    79	decode failure
    80	  -> ProviderPayloadInvalid
    81	timeout
    82	  -> OperationTimedOut
    83	```
    84	
    85	Keep retry policy based on the domain tag, not provider message string matching.
    86	
    87	## Recovery
    88	
    89	Use exhaustive tag matching at a recovery boundary. Recover only the cases the boundary owns.
    90	
    91	- Missing may become Option at a query boundary.
    92	- Conflict may trigger a readback.
    93	- Unavailable may retry under a bounded Schedule.
    94	- PermissionDenied should usually fail immediately.
    95	- PayloadInvalid should fail closed and surface provider drift.
    96	
    97	Do not use broad “catch all and log” as normal control flow.
    98	
    99	## Cause handling
   100	
   101	Causes contain typed failures, defects, and interruption. Use Effect's Cause utilities for diagnostics and supervision, not as a public response type.
   102	
   103	When logging:
   104	
   105	- log the domain error tag and safe fields for expected failure;
   106	- use a controlled defect reporter for unexpected Causes;
   107	- preserve interruption without reporting it as an application failure unless the domain requires it;
   108	- never stringify an arbitrary Cause into a receipt.
   109	
   110	## HTTP/RPC translation
   111	
   112	Translate domain errors through an explicit protocol Schema:
   113	
   114	- tag to status/code;
   115	- safe client message;
   116	- correlation ID if allowed;
   117	- no internal Cause/provider details.
   118	
   119	Keep the domain error independent of HTTP status so the same service works in CLI, queue, test, and RPC contexts.
   120	
   121	## Tests
   122	
   123	Test:
   124	
   125	- every tag is constructible only with valid safe fields;
   126	- low-level errors map to the expected tag;
   127	- retry policy covers only retryable tags;
   128	- interruption is not swallowed;
   129	- public encoding omits secret/internal fields;
   130	- exhaustive matching fails compilation when a tag is added.
     1	# Scope, Time, Retry, and Interruption
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Scope and resources](#scope-and-resources)
     6	- [Finalisers](#finalisers)
     7	- [Time](#time)
     8	- [Timeout](#timeout)
     9	- [Retry](#retry)
    10	- [Polling](#polling)
    11	- [Interruption](#interruption)
    12	- [Randomness and identifiers](#randomness-and-identifiers)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Scope and resources
    16	
    17	Use scoped acquisition for:
    18	
    19	- files;
    20	- sockets;
    21	- database connections/transactions;
    22	- provider clients with shutdown;
    23	- servers;
    24	- temporary directories;
    25	- telemetry exporters;
    26	- subscriptions;
    27	- runtime bridges.
    28	
    29	Acquire, use, and release through Effect's scoped resource APIs. Release must run on success, typed failure, defect, and interruption.
    30	
    31	Do not spread `try/finally` across domain code.
    32	
    33	## Finalisers
    34	
    35	Finalisers should:
    36	
    37	- be idempotent where possible;
    38	- be bounded by timeout where hanging is possible;
    39	- avoid creating new unowned background work;
    40	- log safe result;
    41	- preserve important cleanup failure without hiding the original Cause.
    42	
    43	Define ordering for nested resources.
    44	
    45	## Time
    46	
    47	Use Clock and Duration for:
    48	
    49	- current time;
    50	- elapsed duration;
    51	- deadlines;
    52	- sleep;
    53	- cache expiry;
    54	- polling;
    55	- timestamps in domain values;
    56	- tests.
    57	
    58	Do not use `Date.now`, `new Date()` as an ambient clock, or raw millisecond arithmetic in workflows.
    59	
    60	Parsing/formatting a provided Date/ISO value may remain pure after Schema decode.
    61	
    62	## Timeout
    63	
    64	Every external operation should have an explicit timeout policy derived from domain/config:
    65	
    66	- connection/request;
    67	- provider reconciliation;
    68	- readback polling;
    69	- shutdown;
    70	- public journey.
    71	
    72	Map timeout to a tagged domain error when expected. Preserve interruption semantics.
    73	For HTTP/RPC reads, wrap the complete native operation, including decoded body,
    74	with one deadline. Do not restart the budget when headers arrive. Test a late
    75	header followed by a stalled body using TestClock, plus interruption before the
    76	deadline and release of the pending request/body. A caller cancelling earlier
    77	must remain interruption rather than become a timeout or availability error.
    78	Choose the client budget from the backend's work limit and reply overhead;
    79	DAW's 40-second example is not a universal client default.
    80	
    81	## Retry
    82	
    83	Use Schedule to encode:
    84	
    85	- maximum attempts or elapsed time;
    86	- exponential/fixed delay;
    87	- jitter where appropriate;
    88	- retryable error predicate;
    89	- provider retry-after information if safely available;
    90	- observation/log/metric per attempt.
    91	
    92	Never retry:
    93	
    94	- invalid input;
    95	- permission denied;
    96	- known entitlement/capacity block;
    97	- destructive ambiguity;
    98	- non-idempotent mutation without readback.
    99	
   100	For uncertain writes, read before retry.
   101	
   102	## Polling
   103	
   104	Poll using Schedule and a semantic read operation. Define terminal states, timeout, and contradiction handling.
   105	
   106	Stop when:
   107	
   108	- desired state observed;
   109	- terminal failure observed;
   110	- identity contradicts expectation;
   111	- bounded timeout reached.
   112	
   113	Do not wait indefinitely for an external entitlement/capability change.
   114	
   115	## Interruption
   116	
   117	Assume Effects can be interrupted at every asynchronous boundary.
   118	
   119	Design:
   120	
   121	- which work is interruptible;
   122	- critical region only where necessary;
   123	- cleanup on interruption;
   124	- whether external mutation may have committed;
   125	- readback/recovery after interruption;
   126	- child fibre propagation.
   127	
   128	Do not mark a whole workflow uninterruptible for convenience.
   129	
   130	## Randomness and identifiers
   131	
   132	Use Effect Random or an injected identifier service for nondeterministic values. For provider idempotency/logical identity, prefer deterministic derivation from stable inputs when possible.
   133	
   134	Tests provide deterministic randomness/identifier Layers.
   135	
   136	## Tests
   137	
   138	Use TestClock to prove:
   139	
   140	- retry schedule;
   141	- timeout;
   142	- polling;
   143	- expiry;
   144	- delayed queue/stream behaviour;
   145	- finaliser timing.
   146	
   147	Interrupt at controlled points to prove cleanup and uncertain-write recovery.
     1	# Fibres, Queues, and Streams
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Structured concurrency](#structured-concurrency)
     6	- [Concurrency limits](#concurrency-limits)
     7	- [Deferred](#deferred)
     8	- [Queue](#queue)
     9	- [PubSub](#pubsub)
    10	- [Stream](#stream)
    11	- [Streaming truth](#streaming-truth)
    12	- [Workers and request completion](#workers-and-request-completion)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Structured concurrency
    16	
    17	Every child fibre must have an owner and lifetime.
    18	
    19	Use:
    20	
    21	- fork/join when the parent needs the result;
    22	- scoped fork when the child must end with a Scope;
    23	- supervision for application-owned background work;
    24	- race/parallel combinators for bounded competing operations;
    25	- explicit daemon/background semantics only at an application boundary.
    26	
    27	Reject detached Promises and unowned fibres.
    28	
    29	## Concurrency limits
    30	
    31	Set concurrency deliberately:
    32	
    33	- serial for provider reconciliation where ordering/readback matters;
    34	- small fixed bound for rate-limited APIs;
    35	- inherited/default only when the application policy is known;
    36	- unbounded only with proof that input is bounded and work is safe.
    37	
    38	Do not translate `Promise.all` into unbounded Effect traversal.
    39	
    40	Define failure policy:
    41	
    42	- fail fast and interrupt siblings;
    43	- collect typed results;
    44	- retry individual elements;
    45	- continue with bounded error receipt.
    46	
    47	## Deferred
    48	
    49	Use Deferred for one-shot coordination:
    50	
    51	- wait for server readiness;
    52	- complete a shared initialisation result;
    53	- communicate first terminal outcome;
    54	- test a concurrent ordering point.
    55	
    56	Do not use polling plus sleep when an event can complete a Deferred.
    57	
    58	## Queue
    59	
    60	Use Queue for point-to-point work with backpressure. Define:
    61	
    62	- capacity;
    63	- bounded/sliding/dropping strategy;
    64	- offer/take interruption;
    65	- shutdown;
    66	- work acknowledgement/retry;
    67	- metrics.
    68	
    69	Do not use an array plus timer as a queue.
    70	
    71	## PubSub
    72	
    73	Use PubSub when multiple subscribers need the same events. Define replay expectations, subscriber lifetime, buffer policy, and slow-subscriber behaviour.
    74	
    75	Do not use PubSub for durable delivery unless backed by a durable transport with an explicit adapter.
    76	
    77	## Stream
    78	
    79	Use Stream for incremental, pull/push, or potentially unbounded values:
    80	
    81	- paginated APIs;
    82	- file/network body;
    83	- event source;
    84	- batched processing;
    85	- telemetry pipeline.
    86	
    87	Preserve:
    88	
    89	- chunking;
    90	- backpressure;
    91	- typed failure;
    92	- resource Scope;
    93	- interruption;
    94	- finalisation.
    95	
    96	Avoid collecting to an array unless the contract is bounded and the limit is enforced.
    97	
    98	## Streaming truth
    99	
   100	Prove streaming end to end:
   101	
   102	1. source emits before completion;
   103	2. adapter does not buffer the full source;
   104	3. transformations preserve incremental delivery;
   105	4. sink observes early chunks;
   106	5. interruption closes the source;
   107	6. memory remains bounded.
   108	
   109	A Stream return type alone is not proof.
   110	
   111	## Workers and request completion
   112	
   113	Background work in a Worker/server request must connect to host lifecycle. Use the platform adapter to attach completion and keep domain work as Effect. Do not fire-and-forget a Promise after returning the response.
   114	
   115	## Tests
   116	
   117	Use Deferred/TestClock/controlled Queues to prove:
   118	
   119	- ordering;
   120	- concurrency bound;
   121	- cancellation;
   122	- shutdown;
   123	- backpressure;
   124	- failure propagation;
   125	- no orphan fibres;
   126	- early stream delivery.
   127	
   128	Avoid wall-clock sleeps.

    14	
    15	## Decode once
    16	
    17	Treat all external values as `unknown` until Schema decodes them:
    18	
    19	- environment and platform bindings;
    20	- HTTP/RPC/queue input;
    21	- provider SDK responses;
    22	- database rows;
    23	- JSON files;
    24	- Alchemy state and outputs;
    25	- workflow payloads;
    26	- browser storage;
    27	- durable receipts.
    28	
    29	Decode at the first trusted boundary. Do not pass `unknown` inward for a later caller to handle.
    30	Keep the decoded value typed inside the program. Do not decode the same stage
    31	again or round-trip an internally constructed record just to establish its
    32	type. Pure construction uses the owning types and checked constructors;
    33	additional external input still needs its own boundary check. Encode when the
    34	value crosses an outward contract.
    35	
    36	## Encode owned output
    37	
    38	Use Schema encoding for:
    39	
    40	- provider requests owned by the application;
    41	- HTTP/RPC responses;
    42	- persisted state;
    43	- externally persisted cache entries (an in-memory Effect cache is already typed);
    44	- messages/events;
    45	- workflow outputs;
    46	- receipts.
    47	
    48	Encoding proves the outbound contract and prevents accidental runtime objects, Causes, secrets, or non-serialisable values from leaking.
    49	
    50	## Domain brands
    51	
    52	Brand values that are semantically distinct despite sharing a primitive:
    53	
    54	- account/project/tenant IDs;
    55	- email address;
    56	- absolute URL and redirect URI;
    57	- dataset/dashboard ID;
    58	- stage;
    59	- source revision;
    60	- money/currency;
    61	- bounded count;
    62	- timestamp and duration.
    63	
    64	Do not accept arbitrary strings and rely on parameter names to protect identity.
    65	
    66	Brand at decode/construction. Avoid a public `as Brand` escape hatch.
    67	
    68	Select the native Schema for the source data type before adding domain checks
    69	and a brand. In qualified v4, URL, numeric, duration, JSON, Option and Redacted
    70	codecs already own parsing and encoding. Use native UUID checks for UUID
    71	contracts and retain business-specific checks for other identifiers. A brand
    72	creates a distinct type; it does not validate a format by itself. See the
    73	[native Config and Schema choices](../services/config-and-secrets.md#refine-primitive-values)
    74	and recheck them against the receiving installation.
    75	
    76	## Exact structures
    77	
    78	Use exact object Schemas where unknown keys indicate drift or unsafe input. Decide deliberately whether unknown keys are rejected, stripped, or preserved; do not accept the library default without considering the boundary.
    79	
    80	Represent closed alternatives as:
    81	
    82	- literal unions;
    83	- tagged unions;
    84	- nullable/optional input that decodes into Option when absence is semantic.
    85	
    86	Use a discriminant field for plans, receipts, messages, and errors.
    87	
    88	## Transformations
    89	
    90	Use Schema transformations when encoded and domain representations differ:
    91	
    92	- ISO timestamp ↔ domain instant;
    93	- redacted encoded secret ↔ Redacted value;
    94	- string identifier ↔ brand;
    95	- nullable input ↔ Option;
    96	- provider enum ↔ domain tagged union.
    97	
    98	Keep transformations total in each declared direction or expose decode failure explicitly.
    99	
   100	## Versioned durable data
   101	
   102	Include an explicit schema version in persisted state, events, and receipts. Define migrations as decoded transformations:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	unknown
   106	  -> version discriminator
   107	  -> old Schema decode
   108	  -> migration Effect
   109	  -> current domain
   110	  -> current Schema encode
   111	```
   112	
   113	Do not mutate historical evidence to resemble the new version.
   114	
   115	For custom Alchemy resource props/attributes, use the
   116	[stored values recipe](alchemy-stored-values.md). A codec change must preserve
   117	optional values and protected secrets, remain detectable by the selected diff
   118	path, and support recovery from both saved formats. A successful no-change apply
   119	alone does not prove that historical values were converted.
   120	
   121	## Provider responses
   122	
   123	Provider SDK typings are not runtime validation.
   124	
   125	1. call the private SDK/HttpClient;
   126	2. treat response as untrusted;
   127	3. select the minimal fields;
   128	4. decode through an owned Schema;
   129	5. map codec failure to a tagged provider-payload error;
   130	6. return domain values only.
   131	
   132	This protects against SDK looseness and provider drift.
   133	
   134	## Schema-tagged errors
   135	
   136	Use the installed Effect version's Schema-tagged error class when errors cross serialisation boundaries. Keep fields bounded and safe. For purely internal errors, a non-Schema tagged data class may be sufficient.
   137	
   138	Do not serialise arbitrary `Error`, stack traces, SDK errors, or Causes.
   139	
   140	## Tests
   141	
   142	For each material Schema, test:
   143	
   144	- representative valid decode;
   145	- every refinement failure;
   146	- unknown/missing field policy;
   147	- encode/decode round-trip where applicable;
   148	- redaction;
   149	- old-version migration;
   150	- provider drift;
   151	- maximum sizes and bounded collections.
   152	
   153	Use property-based testing for identifiers, codecs, and round-trips where valuable.
   154	
   155	## One Schema owner and checked construction
   156	
   157	Infer data types from `typeof Owner.Type` and encoded types from `typeof Owner.Encoded`.
   158	Service inputs, results, provider codecs, persisted records and test Layers reuse
   159	that owner. Do not maintain a second readonly interface with the same fields.
   160	Recursive codecs may need one local recursive annotation; infer their other
   161	fields from a shared Struct and keep the annotation beside the codec.
   162	
   163	Reuse child Schemas instead of repeating their string patterns or number bounds.
   164	An ID, source revision, URL, date, offset, span or meaningful bounded text field
   165	needs its owning refinement and brand. Branded strings remain literal source
   166	text: do not trim, case-fold or normalise legal labels as part of branding.
   167	When two fields have an ordering or length relationship, keep one shared
   168	whole-record check. `Schema.Struct({ ...Owner.fields })` copies fields only;
   169	attach the owning record check explicitly to each derived ingress codec.
   170	
   171	Separate three operations:
   172	
   173	- Decode unknown external data at its first real boundary.
   174	- Construct a new constrained value using its owner's `makeEffect` (or the
   175	  installed equivalent). In qualified v4, this checks the type side and fails
   176	  with `SchemaIssue.Issue`, not `SchemaError`; map it to the operation's safe
   177	  named error. Check child brands before constructing a containing record.
   178	- Assemble unchanged records directly from already checked fields. Retain
   179	  business checks such as expected identity, completeness and allowed ranges.
   180	
   181	A typed service input is not fresh unknown data. Do not decode it again to
   182	restore confidence, encode it and decode it to get a type, or copy a codec
   183	locally. New external input still needs checking. Native HTTP/RPC codecs can
   184	own ingress and egress without a second decoder in the semantic service.
   185	
   186	## Optional historical source data
   187	
   188	Domain readers use Option. The source codec owns the saved representation.
   189	For a record key whose source can be omitted or null, v4 supports
   190	`Schema.OptionFromOptionalKey(Schema.OptionFromNullOr(Value))`. The outer Option
   191	preserves omission; the inner Option preserves a present null. A consumer can
   192	flatten these when both mean absence, while encoding can reproduce the source.
   193	If the source does not distinguish those cases, use its simpler matching codec.
   194	
   195	Check known attributes with owning Schemas. Preserve extra JSON only as bounded,
   196	checked source evidence; do not interpret its raw values in a renderer or service.
   197	Check dictionary/rest-field codec behaviour against the installed version rather
   198	than assuming an optional-key codec also works for a Record index.
   199	
   200	Before changing an existing codec, reproduce representative old bytes, encoded
   201	field order, nulls/omissions, literal labels, saved version and cryptographic
   202	hashes. Whole-source and important subsection tests protect different claims.
   203	Effect's ordinary Hash is for collection lookup, not durable source evidence.

    60	Parsing/formatting a provided Date/ISO value may remain pure after Schema decode.
    61	
    62	## Timeout
    63	
    64	Every external operation should have an explicit timeout policy derived from domain/config:
    65	
    66	- connection/request;
    67	- provider reconciliation;
    68	- readback polling;
    69	- shutdown;
    70	- public journey.
    71	
    72	Map timeout to a tagged domain error when expected. Preserve interruption semantics.
    73	For HTTP/RPC reads, wrap the complete native operation, including decoded body,
    74	with one deadline. Do not restart the budget when headers arrive. Test a late
    75	header followed by a stalled body using TestClock, plus interruption before the
    76	deadline and release of the pending request/body. A caller cancelling earlier
    77	must remain interruption rather than become a timeout or availability error.
    78	Choose the client budget from the backend's work limit and reply overhead;
    79	DAW's 40-second example is not a universal client default.
    80	
    81	## Retry
    82	
    83	Use Schedule to encode:
    84	
    85	- maximum attempts or elapsed time;
    86	- exponential/fixed delay;
    87	- jitter where appropriate;
    88	- retryable error predicate;
    89	- provider retry-after information if safely available;
    90	- observation/log/metric per attempt.
    91	
    92	Never retry:
    93	
    94	- invalid input;
    95	- permission denied;
    96	- known entitlement/capacity block;
    97	- destructive ambiguity;
    98	- non-idempotent mutation without readback.
    99	
   100	For uncertain writes, read before retry.
   101	
   102	## Polling
   103	
   104	Poll using Schedule and a semantic read operation. Define terminal states, timeout, and contradiction handling.
   105	
   106	Stop when:
   107	
   108	- desired state observed;
   109	- terminal failure observed;
   110	- identity contradicts expectation;
   111	- bounded timeout reached.
   112	
   113	Do not wait indefinitely for an external entitlement/capability change.
   114	
   115	## Interruption
   116	
   117	Assume Effects can be interrupted at every asynchronous boundary.
   118	
   119	Design:
   120	
   121	- which work is interruptible;
   122	- critical region only where necessary;
   123	- cleanup on interruption;
   124	- whether external mutation may have committed;
   125	- readback/recovery after interruption;
   126	- child fibre propagation.
   127	
   128	Do not mark a whole workflow uninterruptible for convenience.
   129	
   130	## Randomness and identifiers
   131	
   132	Use Effect Random or an injected identifier service for nondeterministic values. For provider idempotency/logical identity, prefer deterministic derivation from stable inputs when possible.
   133	
   134	Tests provide deterministic randomness/identifier Layers.
   135	
   136	## Tests
   137	
   138	Use TestClock to prove:
   139	
   140	- retry schedule;
   141	- timeout;
   142	- polling;
   143	- expiry;
   144	- delayed queue/stream behaviour;
   145	- finaliser timing.
   146	
   147	Interrupt at controlled points to prove cleanup and uncertain-write recovery.
     1	# Fibres, Queues, and Streams
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Structured concurrency](#structured-concurrency)
     6	- [Concurrency limits](#concurrency-limits)
     7	- [Deferred](#deferred)
     8	- [Queue](#queue)
     9	- [PubSub](#pubsub)
    10	- [Stream](#stream)
    11	- [Streaming truth](#streaming-truth)
    12	- [Workers and request completion](#workers-and-request-completion)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Structured concurrency
    16	
    17	Every child fibre must have an owner and lifetime.
    18	
    19	Use:
    20	
    21	- fork/join when the parent needs the result;
    22	- scoped fork when the child must end with a Scope;
    23	- supervision for application-owned background work;
    24	- race/parallel combinators for bounded competing operations;
    25	- explicit daemon/background semantics only at an application boundary.
    26	
    27	Reject detached Promises and unowned fibres.
    28	
    29	## Concurrency limits
    30	
    31	Set concurrency deliberately:
    32	
    33	- serial for provider reconciliation where ordering/readback matters;
    34	- small fixed bound for rate-limited APIs;
    35	- inherited/default only when the application policy is known;
    36	- unbounded only with proof that input is bounded and work is safe.
    37	
    38	Do not translate `Promise.all` into unbounded Effect traversal.
    39	
    40	Define failure policy:
    41	
    42	- fail fast and interrupt siblings;
    43	- collect typed results;
    44	- retry individual elements;
    45	- continue with bounded error receipt.
    46	
    47	## Deferred
    48	
    49	Use Deferred for one-shot coordination:
    50	
    51	- wait for server readiness;
    52	- complete a shared initialisation result;
    53	- communicate first terminal outcome;
    54	- test a concurrent ordering point.
    55	
    56	Do not use polling plus sleep when an event can complete a Deferred.
    57	
    58	## Queue
    59	
    60	Use Queue for point-to-point work with backpressure. Define:
    61	
    62	- capacity;
    63	- bounded/sliding/dropping strategy;
    64	- offer/take interruption;
    65	- shutdown;
    66	- work acknowledgement/retry;
    67	- metrics.
    68	
    69	Do not use an array plus timer as a queue.
    70	
    71	## PubSub
    72	
    73	Use PubSub when multiple subscribers need the same events. Define replay expectations, subscriber lifetime, buffer policy, and slow-subscriber behaviour.
    74	
    75	Do not use PubSub for durable delivery unless backed by a durable transport with an explicit adapter.
    76	
    77	## Stream
    78	
    79	Use Stream for incremental, pull/push, or potentially unbounded values:
    80	
    81	- paginated APIs;
    82	- file/network body;
    83	- event source;
    84	- batched processing;
    85	- telemetry pipeline.
    86	
    87	Preserve:
    88	
    89	- chunking;
    90	- backpressure;
    91	- typed failure;
    92	- resource Scope;
    93	- interruption;
    94	- finalisation.
    95	
    96	Avoid collecting to an array unless the contract is bounded and the limit is enforced.
    97	
    98	## Streaming truth
    99	
   100	Prove streaming end to end:
   101	
   102	1. source emits before completion;
   103	2. adapter does not buffer the full source;
   104	3. transformations preserve incremental delivery;
   105	4. sink observes early chunks;
   106	5. interruption closes the source;
   107	6. memory remains bounded.
   108	
   109	A Stream return type alone is not proof.
   110	
   111	## Workers and request completion
   112	
   113	Background work in a Worker/server request must connect to host lifecycle. Use the platform adapter to attach completion and keep domain work as Effect. Do not fire-and-forget a Promise after returning the response.
   114	
   115	## Tests
   116	
   117	Use Deferred/TestClock/controlled Queues to prove:
   118	
   119	- ordering;
   120	- concurrency bound;
   121	- cancellation;
   122	- shutdown;
   123	- backpressure;
   124	- failure propagation;
   125	- no orphan fibres;
   126	- early stream delivery.
   127	
   128	Avoid wall-clock sleeps.

1	# Schemas and Brands
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4

    14	
    15	## Decode once
    16	
    17	Treat all external values as `unknown` until Schema decodes them:
    18	
    19	- environment and platform bindings;
    20	- HTTP/RPC/queue input;
    21	- provider SDK responses;
    22	- database rows;
    23	- JSON files;
    24	- Alchemy state and outputs;
    25	- workflow payloads;
    26	- browser storage;
    27	- durable receipts.
    28	
    29	Decode at the first trusted boundary. Do not pass `unknown` inward for a later caller to handle.
    30	Keep the decoded value typed inside the program. Do not decode the same stage
    31	again or round-trip an internally constructed record just to establish its
    32	type. Pure construction uses the owning types and checked constructors;
    33	additional external input still needs its own boundary check. Encode when the
    34	value crosses an outward contract.
    35	
    36	## Encode owned output
    37	
    38	Use Schema encoding for:
    39	
    40	- provider requests owned by the application;
    41	- HTTP/RPC responses;
    42	- persisted state;
    43	- externally persisted cache entries (an in-memory Effect cache is already typed);
    44	- messages/events;
    45	- workflow outputs;
    46	- receipts.
    47	
    48	Encoding proves the outbound contract and prevents accidental runtime objects, Causes, secrets, or non-serialisable values from leaking.
    49	
    50	## Domain brands
    51	
    52	Brand values that are semantically distinct despite sharing a primitive:
    53	
    54	- account/project/tenant IDs;
    55	- email address;
    56	- absolute URL and redirect URI;
    57	- dataset/dashboard ID;
    58	- stage;
    59	- source revision;
    60	- money/currency;
    61	- bounded count;
    62	- timestamp and duration.
    63	
    64	Do not accept arbitrary strings and rely on parameter names to protect identity.
    65	
    66	Brand at decode/construction. Avoid a public `as Brand` escape hatch.
    67	
    68	Select the native Schema for the source data type before adding domain checks
    69	and a brand. In qualified v4, URL, numeric, duration, JSON, Option and Redacted
    70	codecs already own parsing and encoding. Use native UUID checks for UUID
    71	contracts and retain business-specific checks for other identifiers. A brand
    72	creates a distinct type; it does not validate a format by itself. See the
    73	[native Config and Schema choices](../services/config-and-secrets.md#refine-primitive-values)
    74	and recheck them against the receiving installation.
    75	
    76	## Exact structures
    77	
    78	Use exact object Schemas where unknown keys indicate drift or unsafe input. Decide deliberately whether unknown keys are rejected, stripped, or preserved; do not accept the library default without considering the boundary.
    79	
    80	Represent closed alternatives as:
    81	
    82	- literal unions;
    83	- tagged unions;
    84	- nullable/optional input that decodes into Option when absence is semantic.
    85	
    86	Use a discriminant field for plans, receipts, messages, and errors.
    87	
    88	## Transformations
    89	
    90	Use Schema transformations when encoded and domain representations differ:
    91	
    92	- ISO timestamp ↔ domain instant;
    93	- redacted encoded secret ↔ Redacted value;
    94	- string identifier ↔ brand;
    95	- nullable input ↔ Option;
    96	- provider enum ↔ domain tagged union.
    97	
    98	Keep transformations total in each declared direction or expose decode failure explicitly.
    99	
   100	## Versioned durable data
   101	
   102	Include an explicit schema version in persisted state, events, and receipts. Define migrations as decoded transformations:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	unknown
   106	  -> version discriminator
   107	  -> old Schema decode
   108	  -> migration Effect
   109	  -> current domain
   110	  -> current Schema encode
   111	```
   112	
   113	Do not mutate historical evidence to resemble the new version.
   114	
   115	For custom Alchemy resource props/attributes, use the
   116	[stored values recipe](alchemy-stored-values.md). A codec change must preserve
   117	optional values and protected secrets, remain detectable by the selected diff
   118	path, and support recovery from both saved formats. A successful no-change apply
   119	alone does not prove that historical values were converted.
   120	
   121	## Provider responses
   122	
   123	Provider SDK typings are not runtime validation.
   124	
   125	1. call the private SDK/HttpClient;
   126	2. treat response as untrusted;
   127	3. select the minimal fields;
   128	4. decode through an owned Schema;
   129	5. map codec failure to a tagged provider-payload error;
   130	6. return domain values only.
   131	
   132	This protects against SDK looseness and provider drift.
   133	
   134	## Schema-tagged errors
   135	
   136	Use the installed Effect version's Schema-tagged error class when errors cross serialisation boundaries. Keep fields bounded and safe. For purely internal errors, a non-Schema tagged data class may be sufficient.
   137	
   138	Do not serialise arbitrary `Error`, stack traces, SDK errors, or Causes.
   139	
   140	## Tests
   141	
   142	For each material Schema, test:
   143	
   144	- representative valid decode;
   145	- every refinement failure;
   146	- unknown/missing field policy;
   147	- encode/decode round-trip where applicable;
   148	- redaction;
   149	- old-version migration;
   150	- provider drift;
   151	- maximum sizes and bounded collections.
   152	
   153	Use property-based testing for identifiers, codecs, and round-trips where valuable.
   154	
   155	## One Schema owner and checked construction
   156	
   157	Infer data types from `typeof Owner.Type` and encoded types from `typeof Owner.Encoded`.
   158	Service inputs, results, provider codecs, persisted records and test Layers reuse
   159	that owner. Do not maintain a second readonly interface with the same fields.
   160	Recursive codecs may need one local recursive annotation; infer their other
   161	fields from a shared Struct and keep the annotation beside the codec.
   162	
   163	Reuse child Schemas instead of repeating their string patterns or number bounds.
   164	An ID, source revision, URL, date, offset, span or meaningful bounded text field
   165	needs its owning refinement and brand. Branded strings remain literal source
   166	text: do not trim, case-fold or normalise legal labels as part of branding.
   167	When two fields have an ordering or length relationship, keep one shared
   168	whole-record check. `Schema.Struct({ ...Owner.fields })` copies fields only;
   169	attach the owning record check explicitly to each derived ingress codec.
   170	
   171	Separate three operations:
   172	
   173	- Decode unknown external data at its first real boundary.
   174	- Construct a new constrained value using its owner's `makeEffect` (or the
   175	  installed equivalent). In qualified v4, this checks the type side and fails
   176	  with `SchemaIssue.Issue`, not `SchemaError`; map it to the operation's safe
   177	  named error. Check child brands before constructing a containing record.
   178	- Assemble unchanged records directly from already checked fields. Retain
   179	  business checks such as expected identity, completeness and allowed ranges.
   180	
   181	A typed service input is not fresh unknown data. Do not decode it again to
   182	restore confidence, encode it and decode it to get a type, or copy a codec
   183	locally. New external input still needs checking. Native HTTP/RPC codecs can
   184	own ingress and egress without a second decoder in the semantic service.
   185	
   186	## Optional historical source data
   187	
   188	Domain readers use Option. The source codec owns the saved representation.
   189	For a record key whose source can be omitted or null, v4 supports
   190	`Schema.OptionFromOptionalKey(Schema.OptionFromNullOr(Value))`. The outer Option
   191	preserves omission; the inner Option preserves a present null. A consumer can
   192	flatten these when both mean absence, while encoding can reproduce the source.
   193	If the source does not distinguish those cases, use its simpler matching codec.
   194	
   195	Check known attributes with owning Schemas. Preserve extra JSON only as bounded,
   196	checked source evidence; do not interpret its raw values in a renderer or service.
   197	Check dictionary/rest-field codec behaviour against the installed version rather
   198	than assuming an optional-key codec also works for a Record index.
   199	
   200	Before changing an existing codec, reproduce representative old bytes, encoded
   201	field order, nulls/omissions, literal labels, saved version and cryptographic
   202	hashes. Whole-source and important subsection tests protect different claims.
   203	Effect's ordinary Hash is for collection lookup, not durable source evidence.

    13	
    14	## Closed expected error vocabulary
    15	
    16	Define domain errors in `errors.ts`. Each tag should support a caller decision.
    17	
    18	Good tags:
    19	
    20	- `AccountNotFound`;
    21	- `InvalidAccountInput`;
    22	- `ProviderUnavailable`;
    23	- `ProviderRejected`;
    24	- `ProviderPayloadInvalid`;
    25	- `PermissionDenied`;
    26	- `Conflict`;
    27	- `OperationTimedOut`;
    28	- `PersistenceFailure`.
    29	
    30	Weak tags:
    31	
    32	- `SomethingWentWrong`;
    33	- `ApiError`;
    34	- `UnknownError`;
    35	- `OperationFailed` with only a message.
    36	
    37	Do not use an error hierarchy merely to mimic exceptions. Prefer a tagged union that callers exhaustively match.
    38	
    39	## Expected failure versus defect
    40	
    41	Use typed failure for conditions that can occur in correct operation and may be handled, retried, translated, or reported.
    42	
    43	Use defects for programmer bugs or impossible invariant violations. Let supervisors/reporting capture them; do not expose them as normal domain errors.
    44	
    45	Do not catch all Causes and turn them into one expected error. Preserve interruption and defect semantics.
    46	
    47	## Error fields
    48	
    49	Include:
    50	
    51	- safe operation name;
    52	- bounded resource/provider safe ID;
    53	- retry classification;
    54	- status/code if safe and stable;
    55	- short sanitised detail;
    56	- nested domain cause only when it is a closed safe type.
    57	
    58	Exclude:
    59	
    60	- credentials;
    61	- headers/cookies;
    62	- full URLs with sensitive query strings;
    63	- raw request/response bodies;
    64	- stack traces in serialised form;
    65	- arbitrary provider error object;
    66	- unbounded messages.
    67	
    68	## Boundary mapping
    69	
    70	Map low-level errors once:
    71	
    72	```text
    73	transport failure
    74	  -> ProviderUnavailable
    75	HTTP 401/403
    76	  -> PermissionDenied
    77	HTTP 409
    78	  -> Conflict
    79	decode failure
    80	  -> ProviderPayloadInvalid
    81	timeout
    82	  -> OperationTimedOut
    83	```
    84	
    85	Keep retry policy based on the domain tag, not provider message string matching.
    86	
    87	## Recovery
    88	
    89	Use exhaustive tag matching at a recovery boundary. Recover only the cases the boundary owns.
    90	
    91	- Missing may become Option at a query boundary.
    92	- Conflict may trigger a readback.
    93	- Unavailable may retry under a bounded Schedule.
    94	- PermissionDenied should usually fail immediately.
    95	- PayloadInvalid should fail closed and surface provider drift.
    96	
    97	Do not use broad “catch all and log” as normal control flow.
    98	
    99	## Cause handling
   100	
   101	Causes contain typed failures, defects, and interruption. Use Effect's Cause utilities for diagnostics and supervision, not as a public response type.
   102	
   103	When logging:
   104	
   105	- log the domain error tag and safe fields for expected failure;
   106	- use a controlled defect reporter for unexpected Causes;
   107	- preserve interruption without reporting it as an application failure unless the domain requires it;
   108	- never stringify an arbitrary Cause into a receipt.
   109	
   110	## HTTP/RPC translation
   111	
   112	Translate domain errors through an explicit protocol Schema:
   113	
   114	- tag to status/code;
   115	- safe client message;
   116	- correlation ID if allowed;
   117	- no internal Cause/provider details.
   118	
   119	Keep the domain error independent of HTTP status so the same service works in CLI, queue, test, and RPC contexts.
   120	
   121	## Tests
   122	
   123	Test:
   124	
   125	- every tag is constructible only with valid safe fields;
   126	- low-level errors map to the expected tag;
   127	- retry policy covers only retryable tags;
   128	- interruption is not swallowed;
   129	- public encoding omits secret/internal fields;
   130	- exhaustive matching fails compilation when a tag is added.
