1	# Errors and Causes
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Closed expected error vocabulary](#closed-expected-error-vocabulary)
     6	- [Expected failure versus defect](#expected-failure-versus-defect)
     7	- [Error fields](#error-fields)
     8	- [Boundary mapping](#boundary-mapping)
     9	- [Recovery](#recovery)
    10	- [Cause handling](#cause-handling)
    11	- [HTTP RPC translation](#httprpc-translation)
    12	- [Tests](#tests)
    13	
    14	## Closed expected error vocabulary
    15	
    16	Define domain errors in `errors.ts`. Each tag should support a caller decision.
    17	
    18	Good tags:
    19	
    20	- `AccountNotFound`;
    21	- `InvalidAccountInput`;
    22	- `ProviderUnavailable`;
    23	- `ProviderRejected`;
    24	- `ProviderPayloadInvalid`;
    25	- `PermissionDenied`;
    26	- `Conflict`;
    27	- `OperationTimedOut`;
    28	- `PersistenceFailure`.
    29	
    30	Weak tags:
    31	
    32	- `SomethingWentWrong`;
    33	- `ApiError`;
    34	- `UnknownError`;
    35	- `OperationFailed` with only a message.
    36	
    37	Do not use an error hierarchy merely to mimic exceptions. Prefer a tagged union that callers exhaustively match.
    38	
    39	## Expected failure versus defect
    40	
    41	Use typed failure for conditions that can occur in correct operation and may be handled, retried, translated, or reported.
    42	
    43	Use defects for programmer bugs or impossible invariant violations. Let supervisors/reporting capture them; do not expose them as normal domain errors.
    44	
    45	Do not catch all Causes and turn them into one expected error. Preserve interruption and defect semantics.
    46	
    47	## Error fields
    48	
    49	Include:
    50	
    51	- safe operation name;
    52	- bounded resource/provider safe ID;
    53	- retry classification;
    54	- status/code if safe and stable;
    55	- short sanitised detail;
    56	- nested domain cause only when it is a closed safe type.
    57	
    58	Exclude:
    59	
    60	- credentials;
    61	- headers/cookies;
    62	- full URLs with sensitive query strings;
    63	- raw request/response bodies;
    64	- stack traces in serialised form;
    65	- arbitrary provider error object;
    66	- unbounded messages.
    67	
    68	## Boundary mapping
    69	
    70	Map low-level errors once:
    71	
    72	```text
    73	transport failure
    74	  -> ProviderUnavailable
    75	HTTP 401/403
    76	  -> PermissionDenied
    77	HTTP 409
    78	  -> Conflict
    79	decode failure
    80	  -> ProviderPayloadInvalid
    81	timeout
    82	  -> OperationTimedOut
    83	```
    84	
    85	Keep retry policy based on the domain tag, not provider message string matching.
    86	
    87	## Recovery
    88	
    89	Use exhaustive tag matching at a recovery boundary. Recover only the cases the boundary owns.
    90	
    91	- Missing may become Option at a query boundary.
    92	- Conflict may trigger a readback.
    93	- Unavailable may retry under a bounded Schedule.
    94	- PermissionDenied should usually fail immediately.
    95	- PayloadInvalid should fail closed and surface provider drift.
    96	
    97	Do not use broad “catch all and log” as normal control flow.
    98	
    99	## Cause handling
   100	
   101	Causes contain typed failures, defects, and interruption. Use Effect's Cause utilities for diagnostics and supervision, not as a public response type.
   102	
   103	When logging:
   104	
   105	- log the domain error tag and safe fields for expected failure;
   106	- use a controlled defect reporter for unexpected Causes;
   107	- preserve interruption without reporting it as an application failure unless the domain requires it;
   108	- never stringify an arbitrary Cause into a receipt.
   109	
   110	## HTTP/RPC translation
   111	
   112	Translate domain errors through an explicit protocol Schema:
   113	
   114	- tag to status/code;
   115	- safe client message;
   116	- correlation ID if allowed;
   117	- no internal Cause/provider details.
   118	
   119	Keep the domain error independent of HTTP status so the same service works in CLI, queue, test, and RPC contexts.
   120	
   121	## Tests
   122	
   123	Test:
   124	
   125	- every tag is constructible only with valid safe fields;
   126	- low-level errors map to the expected tag;
   127	- retry policy covers only retryable tags;
   128	- interruption is not swallowed;
   129	- public encoding omits secret/internal fields;
   130	- exhaustive matching fails compilation when a tag is added.
     1	# Scope, Time, Retry, and Interruption
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Scope and resources](#scope-and-resources)
     6	- [Finalisers](#finalisers)
     7	- [Time](#time)
     8	- [Timeout](#timeout)
     9	- [Retry](#retry)
    10	- [Polling](#polling)
    11	- [Interruption](#interruption)
    12	- [Randomness and identifiers](#randomness-and-identifiers)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Scope and resources
    16	
    17	Use scoped acquisition for:
    18	
    19	- files;
    20	- sockets;
    21	- database connections/transactions;
    22	- provider clients with shutdown;
    23	- servers;
    24	- temporary directories;
    25	- telemetry exporters;
    26	- subscriptions;
    27	- runtime bridges.
    28	
    29	Acquire, use, and release through Effect's scoped resource APIs. Release must run on success, typed failure, defect, and interruption.
    30	
    31	Do not spread `try/finally` across domain code.
    32	
    33	## Finalisers
    34	
    35	Finalisers should:
    36	
    37	- be idempotent where possible;
    38	- be bounded by timeout where hanging is possible;
    39	- avoid creating new unowned background work;
    40	- log safe result;
    41	- preserve important cleanup failure without hiding the original Cause.
    42	
    43	Define ordering for nested resources.
    44	
    45	## Time
    46	
    47	Use Clock and Duration for:
    48	
    49	- current time;
    50	- elapsed duration;
    51	- deadlines;
    52	- sleep;
    53	- cache expiry;
    54	- polling;
    55	- timestamps in domain values;
    56	- tests.
    57	
    58	Do not use `Date.now`, `new Date()` as an ambient clock, or raw millisecond arithmetic in workflows.
    59	
    60	Parsing/formatting a provided Date/ISO value may remain pure after Schema decode.
    61	
    62	## Timeout
    63	
    64	Every external operation should have an explicit timeout policy derived from domain/config:
    65	
    66	- connection/request;
    67	- provider reconciliation;
    68	- readback polling;
    69	- shutdown;
    70	- public journey.
    71	
    72	Map timeout to a tagged domain error when expected. Preserve interruption semantics.
    73	For HTTP/RPC reads, wrap the complete native operation, including decoded body,
    74	with one deadline. Do not restart the budget when headers arrive. Test a late
    75	header followed by a stalled body using TestClock, plus interruption before the
    76	deadline and release of the pending request/body. A caller cancelling earlier
    77	must remain interruption rather than become a timeout or availability error.
    78	Choose the client budget from the backend's work limit and reply overhead;
    79	DAW's 40-second example is not a universal client default.
    80	
    81	## Retry
    82	
    83	Use Schedule to encode:
    84	
    85	- maximum attempts or elapsed time;
    86	- exponential/fixed delay;
    87	- jitter where appropriate;
    88	- retryable error predicate;
    89	- provider retry-after information if safely available;
    90	- observation/log/metric per attempt.
    91	
    92	Never retry:
    93	
    94	- invalid input;
    95	- permission denied;
    96	- known entitlement/capacity block;
    97	- destructive ambiguity;
    98	- non-idempotent mutation without readback.
    99	
   100	For uncertain writes, read before retry.
   101	
   102	## Polling
   103	
   104	Poll using Schedule and a semantic read operation. Define terminal states, timeout, and contradiction handling.
   105	
   106	Stop when:
   107	
   108	- desired state observed;
   109	- terminal failure observed;
   110	- identity contradicts expectation;
   111	- bounded timeout reached.
   112	
   113	Do not wait indefinitely for an external entitlement/capability change.
   114	
   115	## Interruption
   116	
   117	Assume Effects can be interrupted at every asynchronous boundary.
   118	
   119	Design:
   120	
   121	- which work is interruptible;
   122	- critical region only where necessary;
   123	- cleanup on interruption;
   124	- whether external mutation may have committed;
   125	- readback/recovery after interruption;
   126	- child fibre propagation.
   127	
   128	Do not mark a whole workflow uninterruptible for convenience.
   129	
   130	## Randomness and identifiers
   131	
   132	Use Effect Random or an injected identifier service for nondeterministic values. For provider idempotency/logical identity, prefer deterministic derivation from stable inputs when possible.
   133	
   134	Tests provide deterministic randomness/identifier Layers.
   135	
   136	## Tests
   137	
   138	Use TestClock to prove:
   139	
   140	- retry schedule;
   141	- timeout;
   142	- polling;
   143	- expiry;
   144	- delayed queue/stream behaviour;
   145	- finaliser timing.
   146	
   147	Interrupt at controlled points to prove cleanup and uncertain-write recovery.

    61	- headers/cookies;
    62	- full URLs with sensitive query strings;
    63	- raw request/response bodies;
    64	- stack traces in serialised form;
    65	- arbitrary provider error object;
    66	- unbounded messages.
    67	
    68	## Boundary mapping
    69	
    70	Map low-level errors once:
    71	
    72	```text
    73	transport failure
    74	  -> ProviderUnavailable
    75	HTTP 401/403
    76	  -> PermissionDenied
    77	HTTP 409
    78	  -> Conflict
    79	decode failure
    80	  -> ProviderPayloadInvalid
    81	timeout
    82	  -> OperationTimedOut
    83	```
    84	
    85	Keep retry policy based on the domain tag, not provider message string matching.
    86	
    87	## Recovery
    88	
    89	Use exhaustive tag matching at a recovery boundary. Recover only the cases the boundary owns.
    90	
    91	- Missing may become Option at a query boundary.
    92	- Conflict may trigger a readback.
    93	- Unavailable may retry under a bounded Schedule.
    94	- PermissionDenied should usually fail immediately.
    95	- PayloadInvalid should fail closed and surface provider drift.
    96	
    97	Do not use broad “catch all and log” as normal control flow.
    98	
    99	## Cause handling
   100	
   101	Causes contain typed failures, defects, and interruption. Use Effect's Cause utilities for diagnostics and supervision, not as a public response type.
   102	
   103	When logging:
   104	
   105	- log the domain error tag and safe fields for expected failure;
   106	- use a controlled defect reporter for unexpected Causes;
   107	- preserve interruption without reporting it as an application failure unless the domain requires it;
   108	- never stringify an arbitrary Cause into a receipt.
   109	
   110	## HTTP/RPC translation
   111	
   112	Translate domain errors through an explicit protocol Schema:
   113	
   114	- tag to status/code;
   115	- safe client message;
   116	- correlation ID if allowed;
   117	- no internal Cause/provider details.
   118	
   119	Keep the domain error independent of HTTP status so the same service works in CLI, queue, test, and RPC contexts.
   120	
   121	## Tests
   122	
   123	Test:
   124	
   125	- every tag is constructible only with valid safe fields;
   126	- low-level errors map to the expected tag;
   127	- retry policy covers only retryable tags;
   128	- interruption is not swallowed;
   129	- public encoding omits secret/internal fields;
   130	- exhaustive matching fails compilation when a tag is added.

    14	
    15	## Scope and resources
    16	
    17	Use scoped acquisition for:
    18	
    19	- files;
    20	- sockets;
    21	- database connections/transactions;
    22	- provider clients with shutdown;
    23	- servers;
    24	- temporary directories;
    25	- telemetry exporters;
    26	- subscriptions;
    27	- runtime bridges.
    28	
    29	Acquire, use, and release through Effect's scoped resource APIs. Release must run on success, typed failure, defect, and interruption.
    30	
    31	Do not spread `try/finally` across domain code.
    32	
    33	## Finalisers
    34	
    35	Finalisers should:
    36	
    37	- be idempotent where possible;
    38	- be bounded by timeout where hanging is possible;
    39	- avoid creating new unowned background work;
    40	- log safe result;
    41	- preserve important cleanup failure without hiding the original Cause.
    42	
    43	Define ordering for nested resources.
    44	
    45	## Time
    46	
    47	Use Clock and Duration for:
    48	
    49	- current time;
    50	- elapsed duration;
    51	- deadlines;
    52	- sleep;
    53	- cache expiry;
    54	- polling;
    55	- timestamps in domain values;
    56	- tests.
    57	
    58	Do not use `Date.now`, `new Date()` as an ambient clock, or raw millisecond arithmetic in workflows.
    59	
    60	Parsing/formatting a provided Date/ISO value may remain pure after Schema decode.
    61	
    62	## Timeout
    63	
    64	Every external operation should have an explicit timeout policy derived from domain/config:
    65	
    66	- connection/request;
    67	- provider reconciliation;
    68	- readback polling;
    69	- shutdown;
    70	- public journey.
    71	
    72	Map timeout to a tagged domain error when expected. Preserve interruption semantics.
    73	For HTTP/RPC reads, wrap the complete native operation, including decoded body,
    74	with one deadline. Do not restart the budget when headers arrive. Test a late
    75	header followed by a stalled body using TestClock, plus interruption before the
    76	deadline and release of the pending request/body. A caller cancelling earlier
    77	must remain interruption rather than become a timeout or availability error.
    78	Choose the client budget from the backend's work limit and reply overhead;
    79	DAW's 40-second example is not a universal client default.
    80	
    81	## Retry
    82	
    83	Use Schedule to encode:
    84	
    85	- maximum attempts or elapsed time;
    86	- exponential/fixed delay;
    87	- jitter where appropriate;
    88	- retryable error predicate;
    89	- provider retry-after information if safely available;
    90	- observation/log/metric per attempt.
    91	
    92	Never retry:
    93	
    94	- invalid input;
    95	- permission denied;
    96	- known entitlement/capacity block;
    97	- destructive ambiguity;
    98	- non-idempotent mutation without readback.
    99	
   100	For uncertain writes, read before retry.
   101	
   102	## Polling
   103	
   104	Poll using Schedule and a semantic read operation. Define terminal states, timeout, and contradiction handling.
   105	
   106	Stop when:
   107	
   108	- desired state observed;
   109	- terminal failure observed;
   110	- identity contradicts expectation;
   111	- bounded timeout reached.
   112	
   113	Do not wait indefinitely for an external entitlement/capability change.
   114	
   115	## Interruption
   116	
   117	Assume Effects can be interrupted at every asynchronous boundary.
   118	
   119	Design:
   120	
   121	- which work is interruptible;
   122	- critical region only where necessary;
   123	- cleanup on interruption;
   124	- whether external mutation may have committed;
   125	- readback/recovery after interruption;
   126	- child fibre propagation.
   127	
   128	Do not mark a whole workflow uninterruptible for convenience.
   129	
   130	## Randomness and identifiers
   131	
   132	Use Effect Random or an injected identifier service for nondeterministic values. For provider idempotency/logical identity, prefer deterministic derivation from stable inputs when possible.
   133	
   134	Tests provide deterministic randomness/identifier Layers.
   135	
   136	## Tests
   137	
   138	Use TestClock to prove:
   139	
   140	- retry schedule;
   141	- timeout;
   142	- polling;
   143	- expiry;
   144	- delayed queue/stream behaviour;
   145	- finaliser timing.
   146	
   147	Interrupt at controlled points to prove cleanup and uncertain-write recovery.

    15	## One owner per host lifecycle
    16	
    17	An application owns runtime construction and disposal. A package exposes Effect programs and Layers.
    18	
    19	Typical owners:
    20	
    21	- Bun/Node CLI main;
    22	- HTTP server bootstrap;
    23	- Cloudflare Worker module/handler adapter;
    24	- browser application root;
    25	- test runner;
    26	- Alchemy entrypoint.
    27	
    28	Construct at most one long-lived runtime per independent host lifecycle. A browser and server may need separate runtimes because their environments differ.
    29	
    30	## Adapter shape
    31	
    32	Keep adapters small:
    33	
    34	```text
    35	host input
    36	  -> Schema decode
    37	  -> named Effect operation
    38	  -> provide application runtime
    39	  -> execute
    40	  -> Schema encode / host response
    41	```
    42	
    43	Do not perform domain branching, retry loops, provider calls, or manual logging in the adapter.
    44	
    45	## Runtime composition
    46	
    47	Compose Layers by dependency:
    48	
    49	1. platform services;
    50	2. Config provider;
    51	3. transport/storage/provider Layers;
    52	4. domain live Layers;
    53	5. observability Layers;
    54	6. application services;
    55	7. runtime.

    58	
    59	## Shutdown
    60	
    61	Tie runtime disposal to:
    62	
    63	- process signals for CLI/server;
    64	- framework shutdown/hot-reload lifecycle;
    65	- Worker request completion for scoped work;
    66	- test scope/finaliser;
    67	- explicit Alchemy callback lifecycle.
    68	
    69	Do not leave timers, sockets, spans, or fibres detached after shutdown.

    80	- Preserve interruption/resource finalisers within the platform constraints.

    82

    15	## One owner per host lifecycle
    16	
    17	An application owns runtime construction and disposal. A package exposes Effect programs and Layers.
    18	
    19	Typical owners:
    20	
    21	- Bun/Node CLI main;
    22	- HTTP server bootstrap;
    23	- Cloudflare Worker module/handler adapter;
    24	- browser application root;
    25	- test runner;
    26	- Alchemy entrypoint.
    27	
    28	Construct at most one long-lived runtime per independent host lifecycle. A browser and server may need separate runtimes because their environments differ.
    29	
    30	## Adapter shape
    31	
    32	Keep adapters small:
    33	
    34	```text
    35	host input
    36	  -> Schema decode
    37	  -> named Effect operation
    38	  -> provide application runtime
    39	  -> execute
    40	  -> Schema encode / host response
    41	```
    42	
    43	Do not perform domain branching, retry loops, provider calls, or manual logging in the adapter.
    44	
    45	## Runtime composition
    46	
    47	Compose Layers by dependency:
    48	
    49	1. platform services;
    50	2. Config provider;
    51	3. transport/storage/provider Layers;
    52	4. domain live Layers;
    53	5. observability Layers;
    54	6. application services;
    55	7. runtime.
    56	
    57	Memoise shared Layers according to the installed Effect API. Avoid constructing a new SDK/exporter/client for each request unless per-request lifetime is required.
    58	
    59	## Shutdown
    60	
    61	Tie runtime disposal to:
    62	
    63	- process signals for CLI/server;
    64	- framework shutdown/hot-reload lifecycle;
    65	- Worker request completion for scoped work;
    66	- test scope/finaliser;
    67	- explicit Alchemy callback lifecycle.
    68	
    69	Do not leave timers, sockets, spans, or fibres detached after shutdown.
    70	
    71	## Cloudflare Workers
    72	
    73	Treat the exported `fetch` handler as a host adapter.
    74	
    75	- Decode bindings once into a typed service/Config Layer.
    76	- Keep secrets redacted.
    77	- Use the host's incoming Effect request fibre when it supplies one; otherwise
    78	  run through the application's sole host runner.
    79	- Connect background completion to `ExecutionContext.waitUntil` or the installed platform integration.
    80	- Preserve interruption/resource finalisers within the platform constraints.
    81	- Avoid global mutable request state.
    82	
    83	Separate platform telemetry from application Effect telemetry.
    84	
    85	For the native Alchemy API, build shared Layers in the Worker-instance Scope.
    86	Each incoming request keeps its own Scope, interruption and response cleanup.
    87	The separate TanStack Website owns typed clients and one `runtime.server.ts`
    88	runner; its private binding adapter forwards requests to the same-stage API.
    89	Do not lend Effect Context or request services through TanStack, merge them
    90	into its runtime, or borrow native tracer hooks. The native API owns its request
    91	telemetry. Any frontend host-span adapter needs its own qualified owner and
    92	tests. Follow
    93	[hosted web telemetry](../../../alchemy-iac/references/effect/hosted-web-telemetry.md)
    94	for those separate lifetimes and proof limits.
    95	
    96	## Framework loaders/actions
    97	
    98	When a framework requires a Promise:
    99	
   100	- use one runtime bridge;
   101	- call one named operation;
   102	- encode only serialisable success/error data;
   103	- preserve redirects/responses as explicit protocol values;
   104	- do not return Effect services or Causes to the client.
   105	
   106	Hydration boundaries require encoded values. Never assume class instances, provider errors, or arbitrary tagged objects survive serialisation.
   107	
   108	## Browser
   109	
   110	Use a client runtime only for client-owned effects. Do not ship server secrets, provider Layers, filesystem services, or server Config.
   111	
   112	Web owners use `runtime.server.ts` and `runtime.client.ts`, with imports inside
   113	TanStack's matching environment functions. Runtime permission comes from the
   114	repository's exact allowed paths, not a filename suffix. React owns the browser
   115	Atom runtime and registry lifetime.
   116	
   117	Model browser lifecycle:
   118	
   119	- abort/interruption on navigation or unmount;
   120	- subscriptions scoped to components/routes;
   121	- transport through a typed client service;
   122	- cached state through a declared cache/store service;
   123	- telemetry with browser-safe fields.
   124	
   125	## Tests
   126	
   127	Tests may execute Effect directly through the test integration or a scoped test runtime. Do not make each test recreate unrelated live dependencies. Compose a deterministic test Layer and release it after the suite/test scope.
   128	
   129	## Runtime anti-patterns
   130	
   131	Reject:
   132	
   133	- `Effect.runPromise` inside `service.ts`;
   134	- one runtime per function call;
   135	- global runtime in a shared package;
   136	- environment reads during module import;
   137	- live Layer construction in React render;
   138	- swallowed shutdown/finaliser errors;
   139	- detached Promise background work.
    65	
    66	Brand at decode/construction. Avoid a public `as Brand` escape hatch.
    67	
    68	Select the native Schema for the source data type before adding domain checks
    69	and a brand. In qualified v4, URL, numeric, duration, JSON, Option and Redacted
    70	codecs already own parsing and encoding. Use native UUID checks for UUID
    71	contracts and retain business-specific checks for other identifiers. A brand
    72	creates a distinct type; it does not validate a format by itself. See the
    73	[native Config and Schema choices](../services/config-and-secrets.md#refine-primitive-values)
    74	and recheck them against the receiving installation.
    75	
    76	## Exact structures
    77	
    78	Use exact object Schemas where unknown keys indicate drift or unsafe input. Decide deliberately whether unknown keys are rejected, stripped, or preserved; do not accept the library default without considering the boundary.
    79	
    80	Represent closed alternatives as:
    81	
    82	- literal unions;
    83	- tagged unions;
    84	- nullable/optional input that decodes into Option when absence is semantic.
    85	
    86	Use a discriminant field for plans, receipts, messages, and errors.
    87	
    88	## Transformations
    89	
    90	Use Schema transformations when encoded and domain representations differ:
    91	
    92	- ISO timestamp ↔ domain instant;
    93	- redacted encoded secret ↔ Redacted value;
    94	- string identifier ↔ brand;
    95	- nullable input ↔ Option;
    96	- provider enum ↔ domain tagged union.
    97	
    98	Keep transformations total in each declared direction or expose decode failure explicitly.
    99	
   100	## Versioned durable data
   101	
   102	Include an explicit schema version in persisted state, events, and receipts. Define migrations as decoded transformations:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	unknown
   106	  -> version discriminator
   107	  -> old Schema decode
   108	  -> migration Effect
   109	  -> current domain
   110	  -> current Schema encode
   111	```
   112	
   113	Do not mutate historical evidence to resemble the new version.
   114	
   115	For custom Alchemy resource props/attributes, use the
   116	[stored values recipe](alchemy-stored-values.md). A codec change must preserve
   117	optional values and protected secrets, remain detectable by the selected diff
   118	path, and support recovery from both saved formats. A successful no-change apply
   119	alone does not prove that historical values were converted.
   120	
   121	## Provider responses
   122	
   123	Provider SDK typings are not runtime validation.
   124	
   125	1. call the private SDK/HttpClient;
   126	2. treat response as untrusted;
   127	3. select the minimal fields;
   128	4. decode through an owned Schema;
   129	5. map codec failure to a tagged provider-payload error;
   130	6. return domain values only.
   131	
   132	This protects against SDK looseness and provider drift.
   133	
   134	## Schema-tagged errors
   135	
   136	Use the installed Effect version's Schema-tagged error class when errors cross serialisation boundaries. Keep fields bounded and safe. For purely internal errors, a non-Schema tagged data class may be sufficient.
   137	
   138	Do not serialise arbitrary `Error`, stack traces, SDK errors, or Causes.
   139	
   140	## Tests
   141	
   142	For each material Schema, test:
   143	
   144	- representative valid decode;
   145	- every refinement failure;
   146	- unknown/missing field policy;
   147	- encode/decode round-trip where applicable;
   148	- redaction;
   149	- old-version migration;
   150	- provider drift;
   151	- maximum sizes and bounded collections.
   152	
   153	Use property-based testing for identifiers, codecs, and round-trips where valuable.
   154	
   155	## One Schema owner and checked construction
   156	
   157	Infer data types from `typeof Owner.Type` and encoded types from `typeof Owner.Encoded`.
   158	Service inputs, results, provider codecs, persisted records and test Layers reuse
   159	that owner. Do not maintain a second readonly interface with the same fields.
   160	Recursive codecs may need one local recursive annotation; infer their other
   161	fields from a shared Struct and keep the annotation beside the codec.
   162	
   163	Reuse child Schemas instead of repeating their string patterns or number bounds.
   164	An ID, source revision, URL, date, offset, span or meaningful bounded text field
   165	needs its owning refinement and brand. Branded strings remain literal source
   166	text: do not trim, case-fold or normalise legal labels as part of branding.
   167	When two fields have an ordering or length relationship, keep one shared
   168	whole-record check. `Schema.Struct({ ...Owner.fields })` copies fields only;
   169	attach the owning record check explicitly to each derived ingress codec.
   170	
   171	Separate three operations:
   172	
   173	- Decode unknown external data at its first real boundary.
   174	- Construct a new constrained value using its owner's `makeEffect` (or the
   175	  installed equivalent). In qualified v4, this checks the type side and fails
   176	  with `SchemaIssue.Issue`, not `SchemaError`; map it to the operation's safe
   177	  named error. Check child brands before constructing a containing record.
   178	- Assemble unchanged records directly from already checked fields. Retain
   179	  business checks such as expected identity, completeness and allowed ranges.
   180	
   181	A typed service input is not fresh unknown data. Do not decode it again to
   182	restore confidence, encode it and decode it to get a type, or copy a codec
   183	locally. New external input still needs checking. Native HTTP/RPC codecs can
   184	own ingress and egress without a second decoder in the semantic service.
   185	
   186	## Optional historical source data
   187	
   188	Domain readers use Option. The source codec owns the saved representation.
   189	For a record key whose source can be omitted or null, v4 supports
   190	`Schema.OptionFromOptionalKey(Schema.OptionFromNullOr(Value))`. The outer Option
   191	preserves omission; the inner Option preserves a present null. A consumer can
   192	flatten these when both mean absence, while encoding can reproduce the source.
   193	If the source does not distinguish those cases, use its simpler matching codec.
   194	
   195	Check known attributes with owning Schemas. Preserve extra JSON only as bounded,
   196	checked source evidence; do not interpret its raw values in a renderer or service.
   197	Check dictionary/rest-field codec behaviour against the installed version rather
   198	than assuming an optional-key codec also works for a Record index.
   199

   126	- low-level errors map to the expected tag;
   127	- retry policy covers only retryable tags;
   128	- interruption is not swallowed;
   129	- public encoding omits secret/internal fields;
   130	- exhaustive matching fails compilation when a tag is added.
     1	# Scope, Time, Retry, and Interruption
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Scope and resources](#scope-and-resources)
     6	- [Finalisers](#finalisers)
     7	- [Time](#time)
     8	- [Timeout](#timeout)
     9	- [Retry](#retry)
    10	- [Polling](#polling)
    11	- [Interruption](#interruption)
    12	- [Randomness and identifiers](#randomness-and-identifiers)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Scope and resources
    16	
    17	Use scoped acquisition for:
    18	
    19	- files;
    20	- sockets;
    21	- database connections/transactions;
    22	- provider clients with shutdown;
    23	- servers;
    24	- temporary directories;
    25	- telemetry exporters;
    26	- subscriptions;
    27	- runtime bridges.
    28	
    29	Acquire, use, and release through Effect's scoped resource APIs. Release must run on success, typed failure, defect, and interruption.
    30	
    31	Do not spread `try/finally` across domain code.
    32	
    33	## Finalisers
    34	
    35	Finalisers should:
    36	
    37	- be idempotent where possible;
    38	- be bounded by timeout where hanging is possible;
    39	- avoid creating new unowned background work;
    40	- log safe result;
    41	- preserve important cleanup failure without hiding the original Cause.
    42	
    43	Define ordering for nested resources.
    44	
    45	## Time
    46	
    47	Use Clock and Duration for:
    48	
    49	- current time;
    50	- elapsed duration;
    51	- deadlines;
    52	- sleep;
    53	- cache expiry;
    54	- polling;
    55	- timestamps in domain values;
    56	- tests.
    57	
    58	Do not use `Date.now`, `new Date()` as an ambient clock, or raw millisecond arithmetic in workflows.
    59	
    60	Parsing/formatting a provided Date/ISO value may remain pure after Schema decode.
    61	
    62	## Timeout
    63	
    64	Every external operation should have an explicit timeout policy derived from domain/config:
    65	
    66	- connection/request;
    67	- provider reconciliation;
    68	- readback polling;
    69	- shutdown;
    70	- public journey.
    71	
    72	Map timeout to a tagged domain error when expected. Preserve interruption semantics.
    73	For HTTP/RPC reads, wrap the complete native operation, including decoded body,
    74	with one deadline. Do not restart the budget when headers arrive. Test a late
    75	header followed by a stalled body using TestClock, plus interruption before the
    76	deadline and release of the pending request/body. A caller cancelling earlier
    77	must remain interruption rather than become a timeout or availability error.
    78	Choose the client budget from the backend's work limit and reply overhead;
    79	DAW's 40-second example is not a universal client default.
    80	
    81	## Retry
    82	
    83	Use Schedule to encode:
    84	
    85	- maximum attempts or elapsed time;
    86	- exponential/fixed delay;
    87	- jitter where appropriate;
    88	- retryable error predicate;
    89	- provider retry-after information if safely available;
    90	- observation/log/metric per attempt.
    91	
    92	Never retry:
    93	
    94	- invalid input;
    95	- permission denied;
    96	- known entitlement/capacity block;
    97	- destructive ambiguity;
    98	- non-idempotent mutation without readback.
    99	
   100	For uncertain writes, read before retry.
   101	
   102	## Polling
   103	
   104	Poll using Schedule and a semantic read operation. Define terminal states, timeout, and contradiction handling.
   105	
   106	Stop when:
   107	
   108	- desired state observed;
   109	- terminal failure observed;
   110	- identity contradicts expectation;
   111	- bounded timeout reached.
   112	
   113	Do not wait indefinitely for an external entitlement/capability change.
   114	
   115	## Interruption
   116	
   117	Assume Effects can be interrupted at every asynchronous boundary.
   118	
   119	Design:
   120	
   121	- which work is interruptible;
   122	- critical region only where necessary;
   123	- cleanup on interruption;
   124	- whether external mutation may have committed;
   125	- readback/recovery after interruption;
   126	- child fibre propagation.
   127	
   128	Do not mark a whole workflow uninterruptible for convenience.
   129	
   130	## Randomness and identifiers
   131	
   132	Use Effect Random or an injected identifier service for nondeterministic values. For provider idempotency/logical identity, prefer deterministic derivation from stable inputs when possible.
   133	
   134	Tests provide deterministic randomness/identifier Layers.
   135	
   136	## Tests
   137	
   138	Use TestClock to prove:
   139	
   140	- retry schedule;
   141	- timeout;
   142	- polling;
   143	- expiry;
   144	- delayed queue/stream behaviour;
   145	- finaliser timing.
   146	
   147	Interrupt at controlled points to prove cleanup and uncertain-write recovery.

1	# React and TanStack
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Keep render pure](#keep-render-pure)
     6	- [Server and client runtimes](#server-and-client-runtimes)
     7	- [Loaders and actions](#loaders-and-actions)
     8	- [TanStack Query](#tanstack-query)
     9	- [TanStack Router Start](#tanstack-routerstart)
    10	- [Initial JavaScript and fonts](#initial-javascript-and-fonts)
    11	- [React lifecycle](#react-lifecycle)
    12	- [State](#state)
    13	- [Errors](#errors)
    14	- [Tests](#tests)
    15	
    16	## Keep render pure
    17	
    18	React components should be total render functions over props, decoded loader/query state, and declared hooks. Do not:
    19	
    20	- run Effect during render;
    21	- construct live Layers during render;
    22	- access server Config/secrets;
    23	- call raw provider clients;
    24	- mutate global state;
    25	- create unmanaged Promise side effects.
    26	
    27	JSX and pure view transformations may remain plain TypeScript.
    28	
    29	## Server and client runtimes
    30	
    31	Keep separate composition:
    32	
    33	- server runtime: filesystem/database/provider/secrets;
    34	- client runtime: browser transport, client cache, browser-safe telemetry.
    35	
    36	Never serialise a service, Layer, Cause, Redacted value, or SDK object into hydration data.
    37	
    38	Use TanStack's matching server/client environment functions for runtime imports
    39	as well as the `*.server.ts` and `*.client.ts` filenames. Keep browser globals
    40	out of module initialisation and inspect the built browser dependency graph.
    41	
    42	For an Alchemy-hosted Website/API pair, keep TanStack as the frontend. All
    43	Website server entry points use one runner whose Layers contain typed API
    44	clients, not live backend implementations. A private Cloudflare service-binding
    45	adapter supplies its same-stage API; browser clients use a checked public URL.
    46	The native API owns HTTP/RPC/MCP handlers and executes them in its incoming
    47	Effect fibre without another runtime.
    48	
    49	Do not carry Effect Context through TanStack, merge event services into its
    50	runtime, borrow tracer hooks or add a custom backend Worker around Start.
    51	Preserve cancellation and body streams at the narrow host adapter. Native API
    52	telemetry and any qualified frontend host-span adapter have separate owners;
    53	see [hosted telemetry](../../../alchemy-iac/references/effect/hosted-web-telemetry.md).
    54	
    55	## Loaders and actions
    56	
    57	Framework loaders/actions are host adapters:
    58	
    59	1. decode params/search/body/session;
    60	2. call a named Effect service operation;
    61	3. map tagged errors to redirect/not-found/protocol result;
    62	4. encode hydration-safe data;
    63	5. bridge to Promise only at the required callback.
    64	
    65	Keep retries, provider calls, and business policy inside Effect services.
    66	
    67	## TanStack Query
    68	
    69	Wrap query/mutation functions through one runtime bridge. The query key must use stable encoded domain identity.
    70	
    71	Define intentionally:
    72	
    73	- which layer owns retry: Query or Effect Schedule, not both accidentally;
    74	- cancellation: Query AbortSignal interrupts the Effect;
    75	- error shape: encoded domain/protocol error, not Cause;
    76	- cache staleness versus Effect Cache;
    77	- invalidation after mutation;
    78	- server prefetch/hydration encoding.
    79	
    80	Avoid returning `Effect.runPromise(program)` ad hoc from every component.
    81	
    82	## TanStack Router/Start
    83	
    84	Keep route definitions declarative. Route loaders decode and bridge to the server/client runtime appropriate to the execution environment.
    85	
    86	For serialisable loader data:
    87	
    88	- Schema encode before crossing server/client;
    89	- Schema decode on the receiving side if trust boundary requires;
    90	- represent expected recoverable states explicitly;
    91	- prove all error variants are handled.
    92	
    93	Do not depend on class prototype identity after hydration. Return a
    94	Schema-encoded success/error result for expected backend failures and decode it
    95	on the receiving side. Prove tags and useful fields survive the actual TanStack
    96	transport, including an error response status.
    97	
    98	### Router preloading and freshness
    99	
   100	Set link preloading and loader freshness in `createRouter`, not the Vite plugin.
   101	Check the receiving installation's defaults: TanStack retains unused loader
   102	data for five minutes by default, but ordinary `staleTime` is zero. A cached
   103	page can render immediately while a return starts another server-function
   104	request. Retention does not promise a period without requests.
   105	
   106	For public page data that can be reused briefly, the repository starter uses
   107	`defaultPreload: "intent"`, `defaultStaleTime: 60_000` and
   108	`defaultPreloadStaleTime: 60_000`. Intent preloads on link hover, focus or touch;
   109	the one-minute freshness window applies to both loaded and preloaded data.
   110	Choose route-specific freshness and invalidation for changing or personal data.
   111	Encoded error envelopes are also loader data; account for their retry and
   112	recovery behaviour rather than treating them as successful content.
   113	
   114	Router memory, browser HTTP caching, Cloudflare caching and Effect Cache are
   115	separate owners. A server-function reply marked `no-store` can still be held by
   116	the router. A full reload starts a new router cache. Prefetching moves the first
   117	request before the click; freshness controls repeat reads. Analytics requests
   118	and a route's first JavaScript download are separate from page-data refreshes.
   119	
   120	Prove the behaviour in a real browser: hover before opening a page, return to a
   121	visited page within its freshness window, then return after expiry. Inspect the
   122	page-data requests separately from assets and analytics. A build does not prove
   123	these interactions. See TanStack's official [data loading](https://tanstack.com/router/latest/docs/guide/data-loading)
   124	and [preloading](https://tanstack.com/router/latest/docs/guide/preloading) guides;
   125	reconcile their current descriptions with installed source and types.
   126	
   127	## Initial JavaScript and fonts
   128	
   129	Inspect the production build before changing how code loads. TanStack Start's
   130	plugin already separates non-critical route components in the qualified
   131	installation. Router-only applications need their matching bundler's automatic
   132	splitting setting. Keep optional implementations out of the root route and
   133	other modules imported by every page. A separate file or lazy service acquisition
   134	does not remove a static import from the initial download. Use the framework's
   135	normal splitting and keep necessary matching and loader code readily available.
   136	
   137	Import important font assets through Vite's `?url` handling and declare ordinary
   138	font preload links in the owning route's `head` result. Render `HeadContent` so
   139	the browser sees those links in the initial HTML. For WOFF2 use `rel: "preload"`,
   140	`as: "font"`, `type: "font/woff2"` and `crossOrigin: "anonymous"`. The preload and
   141	stylesheet must resolve to the same asset. Preload only the styles and character
   142	sets used by visible opening content; every extra preload competes with it.
   143	Keep the chosen `font-display` policy explicit.
   144	
   145	For owned conditional head data, prefer a checked Schema constructor with fixed
   146	tags, `Option` and `Array.fromOption`, and immutable `Array` or `Struct` operations.
   147	Do not spread a ternary array of repeated font objects into every route.
   148	Trusted Vite asset URLs need no runtime environment reader or browser global.
   149	
   150	Measure compressed transfer bytes separately from expanded JavaScript size,
   151	fonts and styles. Record Lighthouse's network, CPU and cache settings, and retain
   152	repeated results when scores vary. A smaller download alone does not prove that
   153	visible content appears sooner. Prove the emitted HTML, browser font requests
   154	and route navigation separately from local checks. See the official
   155	[code splitting](https://tanstack.com/router/latest/docs/guide/code-splitting),
   156	[head management](https://tanstack.com/router/latest/docs/guide/document-head-management)
   157	and [Vite asset](https://vite.dev/guide/assets) guides, then check installed behaviour.
   158	
   159	## React lifecycle
   160	
   161	For subscriptions/streams:
   162	
   163	- acquire in an effect/hook adapter;
   164	- scope to mount/route lifetime;
   165	- interrupt on unmount/navigation;
   166	- avoid duplicate subscriptions under development lifecycle;
   167	- encode backpressure/sampling;
   168	- update view state through a controlled adapter.
   169	
   170	Do not launch a daemon fibre from a component without cleanup.
   171	
   172	When Effect Atom already owns browser work, use its runtime and root registry.
   173	An optional registration/subscription pattern is
   174	`Atom.runtime(browserLayers).atom(scopedOperation)`, mounted with `useAtomMount`
   175	under one `RegistryProvider`. Unmounting must release the operation's Scope and
   176	interrupt outstanding work. A browser-only registration has an inert server
   177	counterpart selected through TanStack's environment function. Do not create an
   178	extra ManagedRuntime or an unmanaged Promise workflow in a component. Atom is
   179	not required for purely synchronous local UI state.
   180	
   181	Separate browser work when its dependencies or lifetime differ. Appearance,
   182	local progress, analytics and browser-tool registration can share one runtime
   183	and root registry while using independent resource or action Atoms. Mounting
   184	tools must not acquire an unrelated analytics SDK; using analytics must not
   185	register tools. Share checked root configuration through a data Atom rather
   186	than making local features wait for remote service acquisition. A service does
   187	not automatically need its own Atom: split where independent acquisition,
   188	state or cleanup has a real owner.
   189	
   190	Declare service Layers as static values and supply their checked requirements
   191	at composition. In a resource Atom, native `Layer.build` can build the selected
   192	Layer in the Atom's Scope. Pass its resulting Context only to dependent Effect
   193	operations inside that runtime. An `Effect.provide(layer)` around a short
   194	registration operation can release its private Layer scope as soon as that
   195	operation returns; it does not by itself retain the registered service for the
   196	mounted lifetime. Keep a shared resource Atom alive only when consumers need
   197	one instance until the root registry closes. Registration usually belongs to
   198	its mount, while a reused analytics client can belong to the root lifetime.
   199	Check the receiving Effect Atom version's scope behaviour.
   200	
   201	Independent acquisition does not imply delayed loading. An immediate page-view
   202	action still requests analytics immediately. Any later startup policy must
   203	name its trigger and event-loss trade-off, with Effect owning cancellation and
   204	cleanup. Do not add arbitrary timers, detached imports or another runtime.
   205	
   206	## State
   207	
   208	Keep domain state in Effect services when it is shared, concurrent, or effectful. Keep local ephemeral UI state in React when it is truly view-local and synchronous.
   209	
   210	Do not move every `useState` into Effect. Do move provider/cache/concurrent workflows out of component-local mutable logic.
   211	
   212	## Errors
   213	
   214	Translate domain errors to a closed UI state:
   215	
   216	- not found;
   217	- unauthorised;
   218	- validation fields;
   219	- unavailable/retry;
   220	- conflict;
   221	- unexpected defect boundary.
   222	
   223	Never render raw provider messages, stack traces, or Causes.
   224	
   225	## Tests
   226	
   227	Test:
   228	
   229	- domain service independently;
   230	- loader/action decoding and encoding;
   231	- runtime bridge and cancellation;
   232	- hydration round-trip;
   233	- retry ownership;
   234	- subscription cleanup;
   235	- no server dependency in client bundle;
   236	- independent optional service acquisition and root/mount cleanup, including
   237	  a stalled unrelated service;
   238	- exhaustive UI error states.
    16	8. add span and safe attributes.
    17	
    18	Do not use global `fetch` in domain code. If a host supplies fetch, provide it as the platform HttpClient Layer.
    19	
    20	## Status handling
    21	
    22	Map status/code to a closed domain vocabulary. Do not accept every 2xx response without decoding. Do not turn every non-2xx into one string error.
    23	
    24	Handle redirects intentionally:
    25	
    26	- follow when the operation contract permits;
    27	- inspect manually for redirect proof/auth flows;
    28	- reject unexpected cross-origin redirects;
    29	- never log sensitive Location query values.
    30	
    31	## Inbound HTTP
    32	
    33	At the route boundary:
    34	
    35	- decode path, query, headers, cookies, and body;
    36	- enforce size limits;
    37	- construct a named domain operation;
    38	- map tagged errors exhaustively to protocol errors;
    39	- encode response through Schema;
    40	- set headers/cookies through typed protocol facilities;
    41	- execute in the incoming native Effect request fibre when the host supplies one;
    42	- otherwise bridge only at the application-owned host runner.
    43	
    44	Do not pass a raw Request into the domain service.
    45	
    46	For a native Alchemy HTTP host, keep its HttpEffect contract and let the host
    47	adapt routing failures, defects and cancellation. Do not replace all failures
    48	with 500: a missing route must still return 404. Test the native host adaptation
    49	and select safe ErrorReporter fields separately from the response mapping.
    50	
    51	## RPC
    52	
    53	Define RPC procedures from shared Schemas and tagged serialisable errors. Keep transport details out of the domain service.
    54	
    55	Require:
    56	
    57	- request/response Schema;
    58	- error Schema;
    59	- authentication/authorisation boundary;
    60	- deadline/cancellation propagation;
    61	- versioning;
    62	- payload limits;
    63	- observability safe fields.
    64	
    65	Do not expose arbitrary Effect Causes or unencoded class instances over RPC.
    66	Declared Schema-tagged errors are encoded on the wire and decoded by clients.
    67	
    68	## Shared client contract
    69	
    70	Keep native generated clients private to semantic client Layers. HTTP and RPC
    71	clients implement the same domain service contract as the backend. Decode
    72	expected backend failures with the shared Schema and map connection or invalid
    73	reply failures to distinct named domain-access errors. No protocol error or
    74	unchecked provider payload leaks into UI policy.
    75	
    76	Test syntactically valid replies with the wrong payload Schema, as well as
    77	broken JSON. In the qualified 4.0.2, native RPC reply decoding can produce a
    78	SchemaError defect. The private client marks failure inside only the native
    79	exit reply codec's decoder, before native RPC converts that failure to a
    80	defect. Its semantic operation translates only that private marker to the named
    81	invalid-response error. Keep the native Schemas, Ndjson parser, Protocol and
    82	client; do not replace them with a handwritten protocol.
    83	
    84	Never infer reply failure from the SchemaError class alone. An unrelated
    85	transport or request encoder can fail with that same class and must keep its
    86	original defect identity. Test both reads with bad native replies and an
    87	unrelated adapter SchemaError. Preserve caller interruption and other defects;
    88	do not turn every Cause into an expected failure. Requalify the cached native
    89	exit Schema identity and reply decoder behaviour on Effect upgrades before
    90	retaining or removing this compatibility handling.
    91	
    92	For public, unauthenticated browser reads, omit credentials and reject redirects
    93	so a checked API address cannot silently send the browser somewhere else.
    94	Supply native Fetch RequestInit policy when the operation executes, not only
    95	while constructing its Layer. Protected clients need their own explicit policy.
    96	
    97	A selecting field can identify a response union. Native generation alone does
    98	not give a dependent return type: check the selected response Schema before
    99	narrowing literal/default inputs. See the [format-selected example](../examples/format-selected-client.md).
   100	
   101	For browser clients, test CORS preflight with the actual native request headers.
   102	In the qualified Effect version this includes b3 and traceparent. A successful
   103	server request is not browser-access proof. Remote MCP and Website WebMCP have
   104	separate Origin policies; do not inherit one policy from the other.
   105

    14	
    15	Use Effect whenever owned TypeScript performs or coordinates:
    16	
    17	- failure;
    18	- asynchronous work;
    19	- external input/output;
    20	- configuration;
    21	- resource acquisition/release;
    22	- time, retry, or randomness;
    23	- mutable or concurrent state;
    24	- queues, streams, or background work;
    25	- logging, tracing, or metrics.
    26	
    27	Keep plain TypeScript for total, deterministic leaf computation over decoded values.
    28	
    29	## Boundary test
    30	
    31	Ask four questions:
    32	
    33	1. Can this operation fail for an expected reason?
    34	2. Does it depend on the world outside its arguments?
    35	3. Does it have lifetime, cancellation, concurrency, or state semantics?
    36	4. Does it cross a trust or serialisation boundary?
    37	
    38	If any answer is yes, model it as Effect.
    39	
    40	## Host exceptions
    41	
    42	Frameworks may require:
    43	
    44	- a synchronous render function;
    45	- a Promise-returning loader/action;
    46	- a Worker `fetch` handler;
    47	- a Bun/Node CLI main;
    48	- a callback registration;
    49	- an Alchemy provider callback.
    50	
    51	Keep the exception at the outermost adapter:
    52	
    53	1. decode host input;
    54	2. construct a named Effect program;
    55	3. provide the application runtime/Layer;
    56	4. execute once;
    57	5. translate typed failure to the host protocol;
    58	6. tie shutdown to host lifecycle.
    59	
    60	Do not call `Effect.runPromise` in domain or package code.
    61	
    62	## Explicit exception record
    63	
    64	If owned code must use a normally forbidden construct, place a bounded comment or architecture rule that states:
    65	
    66	- host or measured constraint;
    67	- exact file/function;
    68	- why an Effect API cannot satisfy it;
    69	- how the exception is encapsulated;
    70	- test that prevents semantic leakage;
    71	- removal/review condition.
    72	
    73	Examples:
    74	
    75	- host callback must return Promise;
    76	- generated SDK type contains `any`;
    77	- native Map is measurably required inside one service;
    78	- a host requires one exact writable property during a controlled lifetime.
    79	
    80	React rendering can use Effect Array functions synchronously; it does not need a native collection exception.
    81	
    82	“Simpler” and “the SDK uses it” are not sufficient.

    85	
    86	Use the typed error channel for:
    87	
    88	- validation;
    89	- missing records;
    90	- provider rejection;
    91	- permissions;
    92	- timeout;
    93	- unavailable dependency;
    94	- conflict;
    95	- protocol/codec mismatch;
    96	- user cancellation when domain-relevant.
    97	
    98	Use defects only for impossible invariants, programmer bugs, or corrupted assumptions that cannot be handled meaningfully. Do not convert expected failure to `die` to make a signature look clean.

   101	
   102	Search changed owned code for:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	async
   106	new Promise
   107	Promise.
   108	throw
   109	catch (
   110	fetch(
   111	process.env
   112	Bun.env
   113	import.meta.env
   114	JSON.parse
   115	JSON.stringify
   116	Date.now
   117	new Date(
   118	Math.random
   119	setTimeout
   120	setInterval
   121	console.
   122	new Map
   123	new Set
   124	 as
   125	: any

   127	```

   129	Classify every match. Generated, vendor, fixtures, and host adapters may be excluded only through explicit path policy.

   132	
   133	Strict Effect is about semantics, not maximizing `Effect.gen`.

     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Bun and Node scripts](#bun-and-node-scripts)
     6	- [CLI contract](#cli-contract)

    10	- [Alchemy](#alchemy)
    11	- [Framework callbacks](#framework-callbacks)
    12	- [Tests](#tests)
    13	
    14	## Bun and Node scripts
    15	
    16	Write scripts as flat Effect programs:
    17	
    18	```text
    19	decode argv/config
    20	  -> acquire services
    21	  -> perform named operations
    22	  -> encode/write result
    23	  -> map exit status at root
    24	```
    25	
    26	Use Effect Platform filesystem/path/command/process services where installed. Keep `Bun.argv`, `Bun.env`, process signals, and exit codes at the host adapter.
    27	
    28	Do not:
    29	
    30	- mix async helpers with an Effect main;
    31	- call `process.exit` deep in code;
    32	- throw for usage errors;
    33	- write files through raw APIs throughout the script;
    34	- use `console` for machine-readable output.
    35	
    36	Separate stdout data from structured diagnostic logging.
    37	
    38	## CLI contract
    39	
    40	Decode arguments into a Schema-owned command union. Match exhaustively. Return tagged usage/config/operation errors.
    41	
    42	For mutating commands:
    43	
    44	- distinguish plan/apply;
    45	- require exact authority;
    46	- support non-interactive behaviour;
    47	- produce a bounded encoded receipt;
    48	- expose truthful exit classes.
    49	
    50	## Servers
    51	
    52	The server bootstrap owns:
    53	
    54	- Config provider;
    55	- platform Layer;
    56	- domain live Layers;
    57	- observability;
    58	- runtime/server Scope;
    59	- signal-driven shutdown.
    60	
    61	Routes adapt protocol to domain services. Do not instantiate dependencies or read environment in each route.
    62	
    63	## Cloudflare Workers
    64	
    65	The module export satisfies the Worker host. Keep it thin:
    66	
    67	- bindings → typed Layer/Config;
    68	- Request → decoded protocol;
    69	- one request Effect;
    70	- encoded Response;
    71	- background completion tied to `waitUntil`;
    72	- application runtime reused according to platform-safe lifecycle.
    73	
    74	Model Durable Object, Queue, scheduled, and alarm handlers as separate host adapters calling named Effects. Do not share mutable request state.
    75	
    76	For telemetry, flush through host completion and independently prove backend ingestion.
    77	
    78	## Vercel/serverless functions
    79	
    80	Use the same boundary:
    81	
    82	- one function adapter;
    83	- decode platform request/config;
    84	- run domain Effect;
    85	- encode platform response.
    86	
    87	Do not assume a long-lived global runtime will always be reused, but make reuse safe when the host retains an isolate. Scope per-invocation resources correctly.
    88	
    89	Deployment ownership and provider sign-in belong to `$alchemy-iac`/platform architecture, not the domain service.
    90	
    91	## Alchemy
    92	
    93	`alchemy.run.ts` is an application boundary:
    94	
    95	- decode stage/authority;
    96	- choose state/provider Layers;
    97	- compose stack Effect;
    98	- execute through the required Alchemy adapter;
    99	- return encoded safe outputs.
   100	
   101	Keep provider services, errors, Schemas, and lifecycle in packages/modules. Do not turn the root into a 500-line program.
   102	
   103	## Framework callbacks
   104	
   105	If a framework expects Promise:
   106	
   107	- bridge one named Effect through the application runtime;
   108	- translate cancellation/abort;
   109	- encode results;
   110	- map errors through a closed protocol;
   111	- do not expose runtime/service to framework callers.
   112	
   113	## Tests
   114	
   115	Test the domain program separately from the adapter. Adapter tests cover:
   116	
   117	- host input decoding;
   118	- runtime bridge;
   119	- abort/interruption;
   120	- response/exit encoding;
   121	- background completion;
   122	- shutdown;
   123	- no secret/config leakage.

     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [Structured concurrency](#structured-concurrency)
     6	- [Concurrency limits](#concurrency-limits)
     7	- [Deferred](#deferred)

     9	- [PubSub](#pubsub)
    10	- [Stream](#stream)
    11	- [Streaming truth](#streaming-truth)
    12	- [Workers and request completion](#workers-and-request-completion)
    13	- [Tests](#tests)
    14	
    15	## Structured concurrency
    16	
    17	Every child fibre must have an owner and lifetime.
    18	
    19	Use:
    20	
    21	- fork/join when the parent needs the result;
    22	- scoped fork when the child must end with a Scope;
    23	- supervision for application-owned background work;
    24	- race/parallel combinators for bounded competing operations;
    25	- explicit daemon/background semantics only at an application boundary.
    26	
    27	Reject detached Promises and unowned fibres.
    28	
    29	## Concurrency limits
    30	
    31	Set concurrency deliberately:
    32	
    33	- serial for provider reconciliation where ordering/readback matters;
    34	- small fixed bound for rate-limited APIs;
    35	- inherited/default only when the application policy is known;
    36	- unbounded only with proof that input is bounded and work is safe.
    37	
    38	Do not translate `Promise.all` into unbounded Effect traversal.
    39	
    40	Define failure policy:
    41	
    42	- fail fast and interrupt siblings;
    43	- collect typed results;
    44	- retry individual elements;
    45	- continue with bounded error receipt.
    46	
    47	## Deferred
    48	
    49	Use Deferred for one-shot coordination:
    50	
    51	- wait for server readiness;
    52	- complete a shared initialisation result;
    53	- communicate first terminal outcome;
    54	- test a concurrent ordering point.
    55	
    56	Do not use polling plus sleep when an event can complete a Deferred.
    57	
    58	## Queue
    59	
    60	Use Queue for point-to-point work with backpressure. Define:
    61	
    62	- capacity;
    63	- bounded/sliding/dropping strategy;
    64	- offer/take interruption;
    65	- shutdown;
    66	- work acknowledgement/retry;
    67	- metrics.
    68	
    69	Do not use an array plus timer as a queue.
    70	
    71	## PubSub
    72	
    73	Use PubSub when multiple subscribers need the same events. Define replay expectations, subscriber lifetime, buffer policy, and slow-subscriber behaviour.
    74	
    75	Do not use PubSub for durable delivery unless backed by a durable transport with an explicit adapter.
    76	
    77	## Stream
    78	
    79	Use Stream for incremental, pull/push, or potentially unbounded values:
    80	
    81	- paginated APIs;
    82	- file/network body;
    83	- event source;
    84	- batched processing;
    85	- telemetry pipeline.
    86	
    87	Preserve:
    88	
    89	- chunking;
    90	- backpressure;
    91	- typed failure;
    92	- resource Scope;
    93	- interruption;
    94	- finalisation.
    95	
    96	Avoid collecting to an array unless the contract is bounded and the limit is enforced.
    97	
    98	## Streaming truth
    99	
   100	Prove streaming end to end:
   101	
   102	1. source emits before completion;
   103	2. adapter does not buffer the full source;
   104	3. transformations preserve incremental delivery;
   105	4. sink observes early chunks;
   106	5. interruption closes the source;
   107	6. memory remains bounded.
   108	
   109	A Stream return type alone is not proof.
   110	
   111	## Workers and request completion
   112	
   113	Background work in a Worker/server request must connect to host lifecycle. Use the platform adapter to attach completion and keep domain work as Effect. Do not fire-and-forget a Promise after returning the response.
   114	
   115	## Tests
   116	
   117	Use Deferred/TestClock/controlled Queues to prove:
   118	
   119	- ordering;
   120	- concurrency bound;
   121	- cancellation;
   122	- shutdown;
   123	- backpressure;
   124	- failure propagation;
   125	- no orphan fibres;
   126	- early stream delivery.
   127	
   128	Avoid wall-clock sleeps.
     1	# Policy and Exceptions
     2	
     3	## Contents
     4	
     5	- [The default](#the-default)
     6	- [Boundary test](#boundary-test)
     7	- [Host exceptions](#host-exceptions)
     8	- [Explicit exception record](#explicit-exception-record)
     9	- [Defects versus expected failures](#defects-versus-expected-failures)
    10	- [Strict review searches](#strict-review-searches)
    11	- [Do not fetishise syntax](#do-not-fetishise-syntax)
    12	
    13	## The default
    14	
    15	Use Effect whenever owned TypeScript performs or coordinates:
    16	
    17	- failure;
    18	- asynchronous work;
    19	- external input/output;
    20	- configuration;
    21	- resource acquisition/release;
    22	- time, retry, or randomness;
    23	- mutable or concurrent state;
    24	- queues, streams, or background work;
    25	- logging, tracing, or metrics.
    26	
    27	Keep plain TypeScript for total, deterministic leaf computation over decoded values.
    28	
    29	## Boundary test
    30	
    31	Ask four questions:
    32	
    33	1. Can this operation fail for an expected reason?
    34	2. Does it depend on the world outside its arguments?
    35	3. Does it have lifetime, cancellation, concurrency, or state semantics?
    36	4. Does it cross a trust or serialisation boundary?
    37	
    38	If any answer is yes, model it as Effect.
    39	
    40	## Host exceptions
    41	
    42	Frameworks may require:
    43	
    44	- a synchronous render function;
    45	- a Promise-returning loader/action;
    46	- a Worker `fetch` handler;
    47	- a Bun/Node CLI main;
    48	- a callback registration;
    49	- an Alchemy provider callback.
    50	
    51	Keep the exception at the outermost adapter:
    52	
    53	1. decode host input;
    54	2. construct a named Effect program;
    55	3. provide the application runtime/Layer;
    56	4. execute once;
    57	5. translate typed failure to the host protocol;
    58	6. tie shutdown to host lifecycle.
    59	
    60	Do not call `Effect.runPromise` in domain or package code.
    61	
    62	## Explicit exception record
    63	
    64	If owned code must use a normally forbidden construct, place a bounded comment or architecture rule that states:
    65	
    66	- host or measured constraint;
    67	- exact file/function;
    68	- why an Effect API cannot satisfy it;
    69	- how the exception is encapsulated;
    70	- test that prevents semantic leakage;
    71	- removal/review condition.
    72	
    73	Examples:
    74	
    75	- host callback must return Promise;
    76	- generated SDK type contains `any`;
    77	- native Map is measurably required inside one service;
    78	- a host requires one exact writable property during a controlled lifetime.
    79	
    80	React rendering can use Effect Array functions synchronously; it does not need a native collection exception.
    81	
    82	“Simpler” and “the SDK uses it” are not sufficient.
    83	
    84	## Defects versus expected failures
    85	
    86	Use the typed error channel for:
    87	
    88	- validation;
    89	- missing records;
    90	- provider rejection;
    91	- permissions;
    92	- timeout;
    93	- unavailable dependency;
    94	- conflict;
    95	- protocol/codec mismatch;
    96	- user cancellation when domain-relevant.
    97	
    98	Use defects only for impossible invariants, programmer bugs, or corrupted assumptions that cannot be handled meaningfully. Do not convert expected failure to `die` to make a signature look clean.
    99	
   100	## Strict review searches
   101	
   102	Search changed owned code for:
   103	
   104	```text
   105	async
   106	new Promise
   107	Promise.
   108	throw
   109	catch (
   110	fetch(
   111	process.env
   112	Bun.env
   113	import.meta.env
   114	JSON.parse
   115	JSON.stringify
   116	Date.now
   117	new Date(
   118	Math.random
   119	setTimeout
   120	setInterval
   121	console.
   122	new Map
   123	new Set
   124	 as
   125	: any
   126	Effect.run
   127	```
   128	
   129	Classify every match. Generated, vendor, fixtures, and host adapters may be excluded only through explicit path policy.
   130	
   131	## Do not fetishise syntax
   132	
   133	Strict Effect is about semantics, not maximizing `Effect.gen`.
   134	
   135	- Keep pure Effect `Array.map`/`reduce`/`unfold` transformations synchronous; they do not need Effect.gen. Use immutable values even inside a leaf.
   136	- Do not wrap a constant in `Effect.succeed` unless it participates in an Effect interface.
   137	- Do not create a Layer for a static value with no dependency/lifecycle role.
   138	- Do not split a linear program into tiny helpers just to look functional.
   139	
   140	The goal is explicit failure, dependency, lifetime, concurrency, and observability—not ceremony.
   141	
   142	An exception must name its exact repository-relative file and operation/property.
   143	Do not allow an entire file, glob, filename suffix, tests folder or package to
   144	use mutation or execute Effect. The native API already owns its request fibre
   145	and Scope; return the native Effect handler instead of adding a runner. A

    12	// The shared service budget covers completion and scoped cleanup. Every caller

    14	const withinOperationBudget = Effect.fnUntraced(function* <A, E, R>(

    17	  const started = yield* Clock.monotonicTimeNanos;
    18	  const result = yield* operation.pipe(
    19	    Effect.scoped,
    20	    Effect.timeoutOrElse({
    21	      duration: CalculatorOperationBudget,
    22	      orElse: () => Effect.fail(new CalculatorOperationTimedOut()),
    23	    })
    24	  );

    26	  // Timers cannot pre-empt synchronous JavaScript. Reject a late result
    27	  // once control returns, without claiming that CPU work was stopped.
    28	  return yield* Duration.isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(
    29	    Duration.nanos(finished - started),
    30	    CalculatorOperationBudget
    31	  )
    32	    ? Effect.fail(new CalculatorOperationTimedOut())

     2	name: strict-effect-ts
     3	description: Implement, review, migrate, or enforce extremely strict Effect TypeScript architecture across application, package, script, server, client, infrastructure, provider, transport, persistence, concurrency, and observability code. Use whenever owned TypeScript contains Promise or async workflows, thrown errors, nullable values, environment access, JSON or unknown input, fetch or SDK clients, timers, randomness, mutable collections, state, queues, streams, resource lifetimes, logging, tracing, metrics, tests, service.ts, live.layer.ts, errors.ts, schemas.ts, or Alchemy integration. Enforce Effect-first designs while preserving narrow host-framework runtime boundaries.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Strict Effect TypeScript
     7	
     8	Treat Effect as the application language for every fallible, asynchronous, stateful, concurrent, resourceful, configuration-dependent, or boundary-crossing workflow. Allow plain TypeScript only for total, deterministic leaf computation and unavoidable host adapters.
     9	
    10	Use this skill with repository-local instructions, `$repo-structure`, `$package-structure`, and `$effect-client-wrapper` where applicable. Use `$alchemy-iac` for infrastructure ownership, provider proof, and deployment lifecycle.
    11	
    12	## Strictness level
    13	
    14	This skill is intentionally stricter than ordinary Effect guidance.
    15	
    16	In owned code, do not introduce:
    17	
    18	- `async` or raw `Promise` orchestration;
    19	- thrown domain or expected operational errors;
    20	- raw `fetch` or an exposed SDK client;
    21	- direct `process.env`, `Bun.env`, `import.meta.env`, or platform binding reads below a host adapter;
    22	- unchecked `JSON.parse`, type assertions, `any`, or manual `unknown` narrowing;
    23	- nullable domain models after ingress;
    24	- `Date.now`, `new Date()` as a clock, `Math.random`, unmanaged timers, or sleeps;
    25	- `console.*` for application telemetry;
    26	- mutable local or global collections, loops, reassignment, raw `Map`/`Set`, or detached background work;
    27	- repeated decoding of already checked domain values or JSON keys for an internal cache;
    28	- copied primitive refinements or handwritten data types that compete with an owning Schema;
    29	- generic callback escape hatches such as `request<T>(fn)`, `run<T>(callback)`, or `withClient(fn)`;
    30	- package-owned runtimes or repeated `Effect.runPromise`;
    31	- provider objects, wire DTOs, or primitive configuration crossing service boundaries.
    32	
    33	A narrow host callback may be synchronous or Promise-shaped only when a framework requires it. Adapt it immediately to an Effect program, provide one application-owned runtime, and execute only at that boundary. Document any other exception beside the code with its host constraint, containment, and test.
    34	
    35	## Allowed plain TypeScript
    36	
    37	Keep plain TypeScript for:
    38	
    39	- total pure functions over already-decoded values;
    40	- type declarations and static constants;
    41	- JSX and framework declarations that do not perform effects;
    42	- immutable transformations using Effect Array, Record, HashMap and HashSet functions;
    43	- the smallest adapter signature required by a host framework;
    44	- performance-sensitive native data structures proven by measurement and encapsulated behind an Effect service.
    45	
    46	Plain does not mean unchecked. Boundary data still requires Schema, failure still requires a typed error channel, and effects still require the application runtime.
    47	
    48	Read [policy and exceptions](references/architecture/policy-and-exceptions.md).
    49	
    50	## Mandatory workflow
    51	
    52	### 1. Inspect the exact codebase
    53	
    54	Before editing:
    55	
    56	1. Read repository and package instructions.
    57	2. Inspect the receiving repository's installed Effect version and exports. Research the cloned v4 source when available, record its revision, then check every chosen API against installed source/types and behaviour. The canonical template snapshot qualifies rc.117; it does not choose an upgrade for another repository.
    58	3. Find existing schemas, errors, services, Layers, runtimes, test Layers, and observability.
    59	4. Identify the current package boundary and intended public API.
    60	5. Search the change surface for strictness violations.
    61	6. Preserve unrelated dirty worktree changes.
    62	
    63	When documentation and installed types disagree, follow the installed package, then record any compatibility decision.
    64	
    65	### 2. Classify every operation
    66	
    67	For each operation, identify:
    68	
    69	- value success type;
    70	- expected error union;
    71	- service requirements;
    72	- external inputs that need decoding;
    73	- resource lifetime;
    74	- concurrency and interruption behaviour;
    75	- retry and timeout policy;
    76	- logging, span, and metric semantics;
    77	- runtime owner.
    78	
    79	Use this translation:
    80	
    81	| Vanilla TypeScript         | Required Effect model                                                                           |
    82	| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    83	| `async` / `Promise`        | `Effect`, `Effect.gen`, `Effect.fn`; `tryPromise` only at ingress                               |
    84	| `throw`                    | typed `Effect.fail`; defect only for impossible invariant failure                               |
    85	| `T \| null \| undefined`   | decode once, then `Option<T>` where absence is semantic                                         |
    86	| environment strings        | `Config` plus `Schema` refinement                                                               |
    87	| JSON / `unknown`           | Schema decode and encode                                                                        |
    88	| `fetch`                    | Effect Platform `HttpClient` or a private typed adapter                                         |
    89	| provider SDK               | private `live.layer.ts`; decode every output                                                    |
    90	| filesystem / child process | Effect Platform services in a private Layer                                                     |
    91	| time / retry               | `Clock`, `Duration`, `Schedule`, timeout                                                        |
    92	| randomness / identifiers   | Effect Random or an injected service                                                            |
    93	| mutable state              | `Ref`, `SynchronizedRef`, `SubscriptionRef`; `TxRef` inside `Effect.tx` for coordinated updates |
    94	| `Map` / `Set` domain state | `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `Chunk`, `ReadonlyArray`                                                  |
    95	| event callback             | `Queue`, `PubSub`, `Deferred`, `Stream`                                                         |
    96	| cleanup                    | `Scope`, acquire/use/release                                                                    |

    13

    15	
    16	In owned code, do not introduce:
    17

    19	- thrown domain or expected operational errors;
